title: CNIL, Deliberation 2020-091: guidelines on cookies and other trackers (article 82 of the French Data Protection Act)
takeaway: The guidelines restate article 82 of the loi Informatique et Libertés: reading or writing on a user's terminal requires prior, free, specific, informed and unambiguous consent, continued browsing is not consent, and refusing trackers must be as easy as accepting them. They apply to every operator addressing users in France, including third parties whose trackers a site loads, and exempt only trackers strictly necessary for the service or for audience measurement under narrow conditions. Keep proof of consent available at any time, and treat the July 2019 guidelines they replace (Deliberation 2019-093) as superseded.

title: CNIL, Deliberation 2020-092: recommendation on practical arrangements for cookies and other trackers
takeaway: The recommendation gives the CNIL's expected banner design: a first layer that names every purpose, identifies the controllers behind consent-requiring trackers, and offers an accept action and a refuse action of equal effort, with a refusal remembered so that the user is not asked again at each visit. It applies to sites and apps subject to the 2020 guidelines and is the reference the CNIL uses in its cookie fines. Build banners to it, log consent and refusal, and re-ask no more often than the recommended six-month rhythm.

title: Conseil d'Etat, decision no. 434684 on the CNIL's 2019 cookie guidelines (cookie walls)
takeaway: The Conseil d'Etat annulled the CNIL's general ban on cookie walls in its July 2019 guidelines because a soft-law instrument cannot impose an absolute prohibition, while confirming the requirements of purpose-specific consent, easy refusal and withdrawal, recommended retention periods and information on consent-exempt trackers. The ruling binds the CNIL and frames how French regulators assess walls: freedom of consent is judged case by case. Practitioners can operate a wall in France only where a genuine alternative exists, and the CNIL's May 2022 criteria now set the test.

title: CNIL, first evaluation criteria for cookie walls and paywalls
takeaway: The CNIL sets out when conditioning access on consent can still yield free consent: a real and equitable alternative must exist, a paid alternative must be reasonably priced (the CNIL sets no threshold but expects a published justification), consent must be requested only for trackers needed to monetise the free path, and the paid path may carry only strictly necessary trackers, with separate consent for third-party content. It applies to any publisher serving French users. Document the pricing rationale and audit the paid path for stray advertising or analytics tags.

title: CNIL, Deliberation SAN-2020-012: Google LLC and Google Ireland fined 100 million euros for cookies on google.fr
takeaway: The CNIL fined Google LLC 60 million euros and Google Ireland Limited 40 million euros under article 82 for placing advertising cookies on google.fr before any user action, for a banner that did not explain purposes or how to refuse, and for an opposition mechanism that left one cookie active. An injunction carried a penalty of 100,000 euros per day of delay. Cookie rules fall outside the GDPR one-stop shop, so the CNIL acts directly against non-French controllers. The Conseil d'Etat upheld the decision on 28 January 2022.

title: CNIL, Deliberation SAN-2020-013: Amazon Europe Core fined 35 million euros for cookies on amazon.fr
takeaway: The CNIL found that around 40 advertising cookies were written to French users' terminals on arrival at amazon.fr, whether from the home page or from third-party advertisements, and that the banner text (offer and improve our services) described neither the advertising purpose nor the means of refusal, in breach of article 82. The fine was 35 million euros with a three-month injunction backed by 100,000 euros per day. Landing pages reached from advertising links need the same banner as the home page. The Conseil d'Etat confirmed the sanction on 27 June 2022 (decision no. 451423).

title: Conseil d'Etat, decision no. 449209: Google's 100 million euro cookie fine confirmed
takeaway: The Conseil d'Etat held that the GDPR one-stop-shop mechanism does not apply to enforcement of the ePrivacy Directive, so the CNIL was competent to sanction Google's cookie practices under article 82 without going through the Irish lead authority, and that a 100 million euro fine was proportionate given Google's market share above 90 percent in France, 47 million affected users and the advertising revenue involved. It also refused a preliminary reference to the CJEU. Any operator serving French users should expect direct CNIL enforcement regardless of where its EU establishment sits.

title: CNIL, Deliberation SAN-2021-023: Google fined 150 million euros because refusing cookies took more clicks than accepting
takeaway: The CNIL fined Google LLC 90 million euros and Google Ireland Limited 60 million euros because google.fr and youtube.com offered a one-click accept button but required several clicks to refuse all cookies, which the CNIL held discourages refusal and invalidates consent under article 82. An injunction required a refusal mechanism as simple as acceptance within three months, backed by 100,000 euros per day of delay. The decision is the CNIL's clearest statement that a first-layer reject-all button is mandatory. The CNIL later closed the injunction after Google added a reject all button.

title: CNIL, Deliberation SAN-2021-024: Facebook Ireland fined 60 million euros over the refusal path on facebook.com
takeaway: The CNIL fined Facebook Ireland Limited 60 million euros under article 82 because facebook.com let users accept cookies in one click but required several clicks to refuse, and because the button ending the refusal path was labelled Accept cookies, which misled users about what they were doing. An injunction with a penalty of 100,000 euros per day required a refusal mechanism as simple as acceptance within three months. Button labels on the refusal path must say what they do, and the CNIL has since closed the injunction.

title: CNIL, Deliberation SAN-2022-023: Microsoft Ireland Operations fined 60 million euros for cookies on bing.com
takeaway: The CNIL fined Microsoft Ireland Operations Limited 60 million euros because bing.com wrote an advertising cookie to the terminal before any consent and offered no first-layer button to refuse cookies, while acceptance took one click, in breach of article 82. An injunction required a refusal mechanism as simple as acceptance within three months, backed by 60,000 euros per day of delay. The case confirms that a cookie used for both fraud detection and advertising still needs consent. Search engines and other high-traffic services operating in France are treated as within the CNIL's direct reach.

title: CNIL, Deliberation SAN-2022-027: TikTok fined 5 million euros for a banner without an equivalent refuse option
takeaway: The CNIL fined TikTok Information Technologies UK Limited and TikTok Technology Limited 5 million euros because, between May 2020 and June 2022, tiktok.com let users accept cookies in one click but refuse only through several clicks, and because neither the banner nor the consent tool adequately described cookie purposes, in breach of article 82. The CNIL weighed the number of French users, including minors, and its earlier public warnings on easy refusal. Sites with young audiences should expect no leniency on banner symmetry.

title: CNIL, Criteo fined 40 million euros for retargeting without proof of consent (upheld by the Conseil d'Etat, decision no. 482872)
takeaway: The CNIL fined Criteo 40 million euros, reduced from a proposed 60 million, for failing to demonstrate under article 7(1) GDPR that its publisher partners had collected valid consent for its tracker, for incomplete information (articles 12 and 13), for treating erasure requests by merely stopping personalised ads (article 17), for deficient access responses (article 15) and for joint-controller contracts missing required terms (article 26). An adtech vendor must audit partner consent, not merely contract for it. The Conseil d'Etat rejected Criteo's appeal in March 2026, holding that pseudonymous identifiers tied to browsing data are personal data.

title: CNIL, Yahoo EMEA fined 10 million euros for ignoring cookie refusals and tying withdrawal to loss of email access
takeaway: The CNIL fined Yahoo EMEA Limited 10 million euros under article 82 because yahoo.com continued to place advertising cookies after users refused them, and because Yahoo Mail users who wanted to withdraw cookie consent were told they would lose access to their mailbox, which the CNIL treated as a consent that was not freely given. The case followed 27 complaints. Withdrawal must be possible without penalty to the core service, and a refusal must be honoured technically, not just displayed.

title: CNIL, formal notices to website publishers over misleading cookie banners
takeaway: The CNIL served formal notices on several publishers whose banners made the refusal option smaller, paler or buried in text, repeated the accept option several times while offering refusal once in unclear wording, or left too little visual separation between the refusal link and surrounding text, giving each one month to comply. The notices restate that refusing must be as simple as accepting and that information must be clear and complete. Use the listed patterns as a design checklist: contrast, size and wording of the refuse control are now enforcement criteria in France.

title: CNIL, Deliberation 2025-024: recommendation on mobile applications (amended version)
takeaway: The recommendation, first published on 24 September 2024 and amended by Deliberation 2025-024 of 27 March 2025, sets the CNIL's expectations for each actor in the mobile chain (publisher, developer, SDK provider, operating system and store), including how consent for trackers and permissions must be collected in-app under article 82 and the GDPR. The 2025 amendments are non-substantive corrections and clarifications requested by stakeholders. Apps distributed in France should map SDKs against it and treat it as the yardstick for the CNIL's announced app inspections.

title: CNIL, Google LLC and Google Ireland fined 325 million euros for cookies at account creation and adverts inserted between Gmail emails
takeaway: The CNIL fined Google LLC 200 million euros and Google Ireland Limited 125 million euros for placing advertising cookies during Google account creation without valid, informed consent (article 82 of the French Data Protection Act) and for displaying adverts between emails in the Gmail Promotions and Social tabs without prior consent (article L.34-5 of the Postal and Electronic Communications Code), affecting more than 74 million accounts and 53 million users respectively. Both companies must comply within six months under a penalty of 100,000 euros per day each. Account sign-up flows are cookie consent flows and the same banner standard applies.

title: CNIL, Infinite Styles Services (SHEIN) fined 150 million euros for cookies placed without consent
takeaway: The CNIL fined SHEIN's Irish subsidiary 150 million euros under article 82 because shein.com, visited by around 12 million people in France each month, placed cookies before consent, kept reading them after refusal or withdrawal, and used two incomplete banners that omitted the advertising purpose and the third parties involved. The company fixed the site during the procedure, so no injunction was issued, but the fine stands at the upper end of the CNIL's cookie sanctions. Withdrawal must stop both writing and reading of existing cookies.

title: CNIL, American Express Carte France fined 1.5 million euros for cookies placed on arrival and read after refusal
takeaway: The CNIL fined American Express Carte France 1.5 million euros under article 82 after January 2023 inspections of americanexpress.com/fr-fr showed cookies placed on arrival before any choice, advertising cookies still placed after refusal, and previously placed cookies read after consent was withdrawn. The CNIL noted that the rules were well known from its long-running action plan, and reduced the penalty because the company came into compliance during the proceedings. A mid-sized fine for a national subsidiary shows the CNIL is now enforcing beyond the largest platforms.

title: CNIL, 3.5 million euro fine for transmitting loyalty-member data to a social network and for eleven cookies placed before choice
takeaway: The CNIL fined an unnamed retailer 3.5 million euros for sending loyalty members' email addresses and phone numbers to a social media platform for targeted advertising since February 2018 without a valid legal basis (articles 6, 12 and 13 GDPR), for weak password rules (article 32), for a missing impact assessment (article 35), and under article 82 because eleven consent-requiring cookies were written before any choice and were neither deleted nor stopped from being read after refusal, affecting more than 10.5 million people. Customer-matching uploads to ad platforms need their own legal basis, separate from the cookie banner.

title: CNIL, Deliberation 2026-042: recommendation on tracking pixels in emails
takeaway: The recommendation, adopted on 12 March 2026 and published on 14 April 2026, states that open-tracking pixels in emails require consent under article 82, with one exemption: measuring the individual deliverability of emails tied to a service the recipient asked for, which covers transactional messages such as order confirmations, password resets and security alerts and messages the recipient consented to receive; consent to receive marketing does not exempt any other tracking purpose. Senders must clearly inform recipients about pixels and offer a simple way to object. For addresses collected before publication, senders had three months to inform recipients and give them an easy objection route. Email platforms and marketing teams should reconfigure open tracking to consent-gated operation.

title: Spain, Ley 34/2002 (LSSI), article 22.2: consent for storage devices on terminal equipment
takeaway: Article 22.2 LSSI allows a service provider to store or access information on a recipient's terminal only after the recipient has consented on the basis of clear and complete information about the purposes, exempts storage strictly necessary for transmission or for a service the user requested, and permits consent to be expressed through appropriate browser or application settings where technically possible. It binds every information-society service targeting users in Spain. The consolidated text was last updated on 23 January 2025 and the AEPD enforces it as a leve or grave infringement depending on the breach.

title: AEPD, press release: cookie guide updated to the EDPB deceptive design guidelines, compliance by 11 January 2024
takeaway: The AEPD announced that its cookie guide now incorporates EDPB Guidelines 03/2022 on deceptive design: accept and reject actions must be presented in a prominent place and format, rejection cannot be harder than acceptance, access may be conditioned on consent only where an alternative access route exists (which need not be free), and personalisation chosen by the user is technical while personalisation decided by the publisher needs an accept or reject choice. Sites were given until 11 January 2024 to comply. The July 2023 text has since been replaced by the May 2024 edition of the guide.

title: AEPD, Guia sobre el uso de las cookies (May 2024 edition)
takeaway: The current guide applies article 22.2 LSSI together with the GDPR and LOPDGDD: a reject option must sit at the same layer and with the same visibility as accept, consent should be renewed at most every 24 months, cookie walls are lawful only with clear notice and a genuinely equivalent alternative that need not be free, and access to legally guaranteed rights cannot be blocked. A May 2024 section transposes EDPB Opinion 08/2024: large platforms cannot rely on a binary pay-or-consent choice and should offer a free alternative such as contextual advertising. It is the reference for AEPD sanction procedures in Spain.

title: AEPD, PS/00032/2020: Iberia fined 30,000 euros for a banner with no way to refuse cookies
takeaway: The AEPD imposed the maximum 30,000 euro fine for a leve infringement of article 22.2 LSSI under article 39.1.c because Iberia's banner used unclear wording, loaded cookies automatically without acceptance, omitted first-party and third-party detail and profiling purposes, and offered no genuine way to refuse: users could only accept or be denied access. The AEPD also found that the compliance changes Iberia claimed had not been implemented until after proceedings began, and confirmed the fine on reconsideration. A missing reject option alone reaches the top of the leve scale in Spain.

title: AEPD, PS/00393/2022: Infinity Ecom fined 10,000 euros, including 5,000 euros for non-essential cookies placed without consent
takeaway: The AEPD fined an online shop 5,000 euros under article 22.2 LSSI and 5,000 euros under article 13 GDPR after finding Shopify, Klaviyo, Pinterest, Google and Meta cookies (for example _shopify_y, _gcl_au and _fbp) placed before any consent, with no working consent mechanism or granular panel and a privacy policy missing the controller's identity. The amounts are small but the reasoning is routine: named third-party cookies observed before choice are enough for a sanction. Small merchants on hosted platforms should verify that platform and plugin tags are actually gated by the banner.

title: Garante per la protezione dei dati personali, Linee guida cookie e altri strumenti di tracciamento (provvedimento n. 231)
takeaway: The guidelines, published in the Gazzetta Ufficiale on 9 July 2021 with six months to comply, apply article 122 of the Italian Privacy Code: scrolling is not consent, cookie walls are unlawful unless an equivalent alternative exists, closing the banner with the X (top right, graphically equal to the accept control) must leave default settings in place, the banner may be re-presented only after at least six months or a material change, and analytics cookies escape consent only with IP truncation and no cross-site combination. Every site addressing Italian users must follow them; the Garante cites them in each cookie warning and fine.

title: Garante, provvedimento n. 670: warning and compliance order after Guardia di Finanza cookie inspections of e-commerce sites
takeaway: Under a 2021 protocol, the Garante delegated online checks of a sample of e-commerce operators to the Guardia di Finanza's privacy unit; on the inspected shop the banner offered OK and No grazie but no cookie policy existed and no cookie categories were disclosed, so consent could not be specific or informed. The Garante found breaches of articles 4(11), 5, 7, 12, 13, 24 and 25 GDPR and article 122 of the Code, issued a warning under article 58(2)(b) and ordered a compliant banner with an information layer, without a fine because the operator had partly remediated. Italian sweeps target small sites and turn on documentation, not only buttons.

title: Germany, TDDDG section 25 (Telekommunikation-Digitale-Dienste-Datenschutz-Gesetz, formerly TTDSG): protection of privacy in terminal equipment
takeaway: Section 25(1) TDDDG permits storing information on, or accessing information already stored in, an end user's terminal only with consent given on the basis of clear and comprehensive information, and requires that information and consent meet the GDPR standard. Section 25(2) exempts storage or access whose sole purpose is transmitting a message over a public network, or which is strictly necessary for a digital service the user has expressly requested. The provision applies to any provider of digital services reaching German users, irrespective of whether personal data is involved. The act was renamed from TTDSG to TDDDG on 14 May 2024 with the section unchanged.

title: Germany, Einwilligungsverwaltungsverordnung (EinwV): regulation on recognised consent management services
takeaway: The regulation (BGBl. 2025 I Nr. 32), in force since 1 April 2025 under section 26(2) TDDDG, defines the requirements a consent management service must meet to be recognised (user-friendly and competition-neutral procedures, switching, security concept, a public register under section 13) and names the recognising authority. Integration by digital service providers is voluntary (section 18(1)), but a provider that integrates a recognised service must respect the stored settings and point users to them when asking for consent (section 19), and browsers should not suppress or alter the signal (section 17). The provider stays responsible for GDPR consent validity (section 1(2)).

title: BfDI recognises the first consent management service under the EinwV (Consenter)
takeaway: On 17 October 2025 the Federal Commissioner (BfDI) recognised the first service under the Einwilligungsverwaltungsverordnung, the PIMS Consenter from Law & Innovation Technology GmbH, and entered it in the public register required by section 13 EinwV. Recognition makes the section 18 and 19 EinwV duties concrete for any German digital service that chooses to integrate the service: stored end-user settings must be honoured and users must be told the service is integrated. Consent platforms operating in Germany should decide whether to interoperate with recognised services and document that decision.

title: DSK, Orientierungshilfe fuer Anbieter:innen von Telemedien (OH Telemedien 2021), version 1.1
takeaway: The joint guidance of the German federal and state data protection authorities, first adopted in December 2021 and revised by the 104th DSK in December 2022, reads section 25 TTDSG (now TDDDG) as requiring consent for any storage or access on the terminal regardless of personal data, limits the strictly necessary exemption to functional necessity rather than economic need, and treats a first layer with accept all but no equally accessible reject as invalid consent. It rules out legitimate interest as a substitute for the section 25 standard and refuses to label reach measurement as necessary per se. German supervisory audits, including the BayLDA's, apply it.

title: DSK, Beschluss zur Bewertung von Pur-Abo-Modellen auf Websites
takeaway: The German authorities accept consent-or-pay (Pur-Abo) models on websites only where the paid alternative gives fundamentally the same service at a market-standard price, consent for the tracked version meets every GDPR requirement including granular consent per distinct purpose, and the paid version stores or reads only what is strictly necessary for the chosen service. Blanket consent covering several purposes is invalid. Publishers using Pur-Abo models in Germany should separate advertising, measurement and personalisation consents and audit the paid path for tracking; the EDPB's April 2024 opinion adds stricter conditions for large platforms.

title: Bundesgerichtshof, judgment I ZR 7/16 (Cookie-Einwilligung II, Planet49)
takeaway: Following the CJEU's judgment in C-673/17, the BGH held that section 15(3) TMG had to be read in conformity with article 5(3) of the ePrivacy Directive, so cookies for advertising and market research require active consent and a pre-ticked checkbox does not provide it. The same judgment found consent to telephone advertising invalid where the user faced an onerous opt-out list of partner companies. The ruling ended the German opt-out reading for non-essential cookies and was later codified in section 25 TTDSG (now TDDDG) from 1 December 2021.

title: Landgericht Muenchen I, judgment 3 O 17493/20 on Google Fonts embedded from Google servers
takeaway: The court held that loading Google Fonts from Google's servers transmits the visitor's dynamic IP address to Google without consent, which infringes the general right of personality under section 823(1) BGB and article 6(1)(a) GDPR, and awarded 100 euros in non-material damages plus an injunction. The judgment triggered a wave of warning letters in Germany and is the reference for treating third-party resource loads as data transfers needing a legal basis. Self-host fonts, maps and scripts or gate them behind consent; a banner covering cookies alone does not address the IP transfer.

title: Oberlandesgericht Koeln, judgment 6 U 80/23: accept and reject options in a cookie banner must be equivalent
takeaway: The OLG Koeln held that a banner offering consent on the first layer while allowing refusal only on the second layer, and using an Accept and close X in the corner, gives users no rejection option equivalent to the consent option based on clear and comprehensive information, so the consent is invalid under section 25 TTDSG and the GDPR. The claim was brought by a consumer association under German unfair competition law. Site operators in Germany face civil injunctions from competitors and associations, not only regulators, for asymmetric banners; give both options the same layer and weight.

title: Verwaltungsgericht Hannover, judgment 10 A 5385/22: a reject all button on the first layer is mandatory
takeaway: The administrative court upheld an order by the Lower Saxony data protection commissioner against a publisher, holding that where a banner offers Accept all it must offer an equally visible Reject all on the same layer, that repeating the banner to pressure users and highlighting the accept option violate the requirement of freely given consent, and that information on third-party partners, transfers outside the EU and revocation must be immediately visible. The judgment is the first German administrative court decision on banner design and backs supervisory orders under section 25 TDDDG. Treat nudging patterns as grounds for a binding order, not only a fine.

title: BayLDA, press release on automated checks of cookie banners on 350 websites and 15 apps
takeaway: The Bavarian State Office for Data Protection Supervision announced that it had used an automated tool to check more than 350 Bavarian websites and 15 apps, finding that almost all apps read data before any consent and that the websites' banners failed the requirement that the option to withhold consent appear on the first layer alongside Accept all. Operators were given the opportunity to respond and fix their sites, and the BayLDA said it would extend the tool to further consent platforms. Expect scripted first-layer checks from German state authorities and design banners to pass them without human review.

title: Belgian DPA (APD/GBA), decision 21/2022 on IAB Europe and the Transparency and Consent Framework
takeaway: The Litigation Chamber found that the TC String generated under the TCF is personal data, that IAB Europe is a controller for it, and that the framework breached the GDPR on legal basis, transparency, security and accountability; it fined IAB Europe 250,000 euros and gave two months to submit an action plan, which it approved on 11 January 2023. The decision passed the one-stop-shop consistency process and was endorsed by all concerned authorities. On 14 May 2025 the Market Court annulled decision 21/2022 on procedural grounds while confirming its findings and the fine in its own judgment.

title: Brussels Market Court, judgment 2022/AR/292 on IAB Europe's appeal against decision 21/2022
takeaway: Applying the CJEU's judgment in C-604/22 of 7 March 2024, the Market Court ruled with full jurisdiction that the TC String is personal data and that IAB Europe is joint controller for processing of user preferences within the TCF, confirmed the infringements and the 250,000 euro fine, but annulled the Belgian DPA's decision 21/2022 for procedural reasons and rejected the DPA's finding that IAB Europe is controller for processing occurring entirely within the OpenRTB protocol. Publishers and vendors relying on TCF signals remain individually responsible for a valid legal basis and transparency; the framework alone does not deliver compliance.

title: Belgian DPA, decision 85/2022: Roularta Media Group fined 50,000 euros after the cookie sweep of 20 press sites
takeaway: In its first thematic investigation the Belgian DPA's Inspection Service examined the 20 most visited Belgian news sites for cookie use, consent and transparency, and fined Roularta 50,000 euros for cookies placed before consent, reliance on legitimate interest for non-essential cookies, pre-ticked choices and deficient information and withdrawal on two of its sites, with an order to comply. A parallel decision of 16 June 2022 fined Rossel 50,000 euros for similar practices on three sites. Publishers in Belgium should expect sector-wide sweeps with technical evidence and orders addressed to each violation.

title: EDPB, article 65 binding decision requiring the Belgian DPA to examine a noyb cookie banner complaint against VRT on the merits
takeaway: In a dispute resolution decision adopted on 28 May 2026 under article 65(1)(a) GDPR, the EDPB rejected the Belgian DPA's dismissal, as an abuse of rights under articles 77 and 80(1), of a cookie banner complaint that noyb lodged with the Austrian DPA on behalf of an individual against the Belgian public broadcaster, and instructed the Belgian DPA as lead authority to assess the complaint on its merits and submit a new draft decision under article 60(3). The decision closes the Belgian route of dismissing NGO-backed model complaints; cross-border banner complaints will be decided on substance.

title: Autoriteit Persoonsgegevens, five cookie banner investigations closed after corrections (deceptive banners)
takeaway: The Dutch DPA reported that all five organisations it investigated in 2024, across finance, media and hospitality, broke the law through hidden reject buttons, pre-ticked boxes and cookies placed before or despite refusal, and that all five corrected their banners after its intervention. The AP restated its rules: ask permission clearly without tricks that make saying no difficult, place no tracking cookies without consent, and rely on the exemption only for strictly necessary functional cookies. It announced systematic checks of around 10,000 Dutch websites, with warnings before fines. Dutch-facing sites should expect a warning letter and a short window to fix the first layer.

title: Autoriteit Persoonsgegevens, more than 200 websites warned over misleading cookie banners; three quarters corrected, enforcement against the rest
takeaway: The AP announced that, since it began structural checks in February 2024, it had warned more than 200 organisations about their cookie banners, that about three quarters had improved them, and that it was opening enforcement procedures against those that had not. Its position is that tracking cookies may be placed only with voluntary, informed and unambiguous consent based on clear information, and that the simplest way to respect users' choice is not to use tracking software at all. Organisations serving Dutch users should treat an AP warning as the last step before a formal investigation.

title: Data Protection Commission, Guidance note on cookies and other tracking technologies
takeaway: Applying Regulation 5(3) of the ePrivacy Regulations 2011 (S.I. 336 of 2011), the DPC states that storing or accessing information on a device requires consent after clear information, that pre-ticked boxes and sliders set to on are not consent following Planet49, that rejecting must be as easy as accepting, that analytics cookies need consent even if first-party aggregated analytics are a low enforcement priority, and that consent should be re-affirmed no later than six months after it is recorded. Only communications and strictly necessary cookies (for example shopping-basket session cookies) are exempt. It remains the operative Irish standard for banner design.

title: Data Protection Commission, Report on the use of cookies and other tracking technologies (cookie sweep)
takeaway: The DPC surveyed a selection of Irish websites across media and publishing, retail, food ordering, insurance, sport and the public sector between August and December 2019 to examine how controllers obtain consent for cookies and other tracking technologies, and found that advertising technology and tracking were core to many of the business models examined, with widespread non-compliance. The report was published alongside the DPC's guidance note and framed the DPC's stated intention to examine consent practices. Use it to understand which practices the DPC flagged, then apply the guidance note as the operative rules.

title: Denmark, Cookiebekendtgoerelsen (BEK nr 1148 af 9. december 2011) on information and consent for storage of or access to information on terminal equipment
takeaway: The Danish cookie order, in force since 14 December 2011, prohibits storing or accessing information on an end user's terminal without prior information and consent, and exempts storage or access that is a technical precondition for delivering a service the user requested or for transmitting communications. It applies to any website or app addressed to Danish users regardless of whether personal data is processed. The Danish Agency for Digital Government (Digitaliseringsstyrelsen) supervises the order, while Datatilsynet supervises the subsequent processing under the GDPR; the two authorities' joint guidance of May 2025 explains how the regimes interlock.

title: Datatilsynet, guidance on the use of cookie walls (four criteria) following two decisions
takeaway: Datatilsynet published four criteria for lawful cookie walls after two decisions: one publisher was found compliant because its paid alternative was substantially equivalent and reasonably priced, another non-compliant because the service offered against consent was not substantially similar to the paid one. The criteria require a reasonable alternative for visitors who refuse, a price that does not make the choice illusory, consent requested only for purposes needed to fund the free path (statistics and personalisation need separate consent), and only strictly necessary processing on the paid path. Both publishers received orders on statistical purposes.

title: Datatilsynet and Digitaliseringsstyrelsen, joint guidance on the use of cookies and similar technologies
takeaway: The two Danish authorities issued one guidance document, with a supplementary catalogue of practical advice, covering both the cookie order and the data protection rules that usually apply in parallel: the cookie order requires consent before cookies are placed, and the GDPR governs the processing that follows, including any statistics or advertising. The guidance explains when each regime applies, gives examples of compliant consent solutions and common pitfalls, and replaces the earlier separate Danish cookie guidance as the reference for supervision. Danish-facing sites should re-check banners against it, in particular the treatment of statistics cookies.

title: Austrian Datenschutzbehoerde, decision on Google Analytics and EU-US transfers (noyb model complaint 101)
takeaway: In the first decision on noyb's 101 complaints after Schrems II, the DSB held that an Austrian website's use of Google Analytics transferred personal data (identifiers, IP address, browser data) to the United States in breach of Chapter V GDPR, because the standard contractual clauses and Google's supplementary measures could not prevent access under FISA 702 and EO 12333. The reasoning was adopted by other authorities in 2022 and drove the move to consent-gated or EU-hosted analytics. The EU-US Data Privacy Framework adopted in July 2023 changed the transfer basis, but the analysis of what analytics tags actually send remains the practical checklist.

title: Bundesverwaltungsgericht (Austria), DerStandard pay or okay: DSB decision confirmed, consent must be granular
takeaway: The Federal Administrative Court confirmed the DSB's 2023 finding that derstandard.at did not obtain valid consent under its pay-or-okay model (subscription priced at 9.90 euros per month) because users could only consent or refuse globally, whereas the GDPR requires the option to consent separately to distinct processing purposes; the DSB had not objected to the model as such. The court allowed an appeal to the Supreme Administrative Court on the novel question. Austrian publishers using consent-or-pay must offer per-purpose consent inside the tracked option and should expect a referral to the CJEU.

title: Bundesverwaltungsgericht (Austria), W171 2303402-1: ORF.at must give accept and reject buttons equal prominence
takeaway: The Federal Administrative Court upheld an October 2024 DSB decision, originating in noyb's August 2021 campaign against 422 websites, that the public broadcaster's banner used deceptive design by colouring the Accept button and leaving Reject less prominent, leading to unintended consent in breach of transparency and freely given consent. ORF must redesign the banner so that both buttons receive equal prominence. This is the first Austrian court ruling on button colour and contrast; Austrian-facing sites should remove visual hierarchy between the two first-layer options.

title: Integritetsskyddsmyndigheten (IMY), three cookie banner decisions: reprimands for Warner Music Sweden, ATG and Aller Media
takeaway: Investigating complaints from individuals abroad, IMY reprimanded Warner Music Sweden for not adequately informing users of the right to withdraw consent (articles 6 and 7(3) GDPR), ATG for misleading banner design that hindered informed and voluntary consent, and Aller Media for processing without a legal basis by citing legitimate interest for cookie data without a documented balancing test (article 6(1)(f)). IMY noted that the Post and Telecom Authority (PTS) alone supervises the Electronic Communications Act's cookie rules, while IMY supervises the subsequent GDPR processing. Swedish-facing sites need a documented basis for post-consent processing, not only a banner.

title: Traficom, guidance on cookies and other information stored on users' terminal devices (service providers)
takeaway: Following Helsinki Administrative Court rulings that transferred cookie consent questions to Traficom, the agency's guidance under section 205 of the Act on Electronic Communications Services (917/2014) states that consent for non-essential cookies cannot be given through browser settings, continued use or pre-ticked toggles, must be as easy to refuse as to give and as easy to withdraw, and that legitimate interest is not a basis for storing on the terminal. Only cookies necessary for a requested service (login, security, payment) are exempt. The page records updates through 23 April 2026 and enforcement decisions against major Finnish providers for misclassifying cookies as necessary.

title: Norway, Lov om elektronisk kommunikasjon (ekomloven) section 3-15: cookies require GDPR-standard consent
takeaway: The new Electronic Communications Act of 13 December 2024, in force from 1 January 2025, replaces the 2003 act and provides in section 3-15 that storing or accessing information on a user's equipment is prohibited unless the user has been informed of what is processed, the purpose and who processes it, and has given consent meeting the GDPR's requirements; exemptions cover transmission and storage strictly necessary for an information-society service the user expressly requested. Browser settings no longer count as consent in Norway. Datatilsynet and Nkom share supervision: Nkom decides scope and exemptions, Datatilsynet decides information and consent validity.

title: Datatilsynet (Norway), guidance on consent for cookies and other tracking technologies: ten practical rules
takeaway: Applying ekomloven section 3-15, the guidance sets ten rules for a valid banner: clear information in the consent box, full information behind it, no conditioning of access on consent, per-purpose choice, no pre-ticked boxes or acceptance by passivity, refusal without extra clicks, no hiding or de-emphasising the reject option, plain wording on buttons, easy withdrawal, and internal control of what the site sets. It states that other GDPR bases can almost never replace consent for the subsequent processing of cookie data. The current version, updated in April 2025, replaces the 2023 guidance that first demanded an equal reject option.

title: UODO, bulletin 03/2025: the Polish DPA's position on cookie consent and banners
takeaway: The Polish supervisory authority's March 2025 bulletin states that consent to cookies must be voluntary, informed, unambiguous and preceded by an active user action, that pre-ticked boxes are invalid, that rejecting must be as easy as accepting, that cookie walls which block content unless all cookies are accepted are incompatible with freely given consent, and that clear pre-consent information on data and purposes is required; it relies on EDPB Guidelines 05/2020 and the CJEU judgments in Planet49 (C-673/17) and Orange Romania (C-61/19). Poland has no separate cookie regulator, so UODO applies the GDPR standard to banners directly.

title: CNPD (Luxembourg), updated guidelines on cookies and other tracking devices
takeaway: The CNPD published an updated set of guidelines, in French, for operators of websites and applications on the use of cookies and other tracking devices, distinguishing essential cookies that need no consent from non-essential cookies that require prior informed consent, and accompanied by a practical fact sheet for the public and for operators. The guidelines are the CNPD's stated reference for compliance in Luxembourg and are aligned with the CJEU and EDPB positions. Operators established in Luxembourg, including many EU headquarters of platforms, should map their banners to the guidelines' categories.

title: Hellenic DPA, Recommendations 1/2020 on compliance of controllers with the electronic communications legislation for trackers
takeaway: Issued after an audit of popular Greek websites found widespread non-compliance, the recommendations under Law 3471/2006 require prior consent for every tracker not technically necessary, including third-party analytics, with a two-month grace period. Accepting and refusing must take the same number of clicks from the same layer, withdrawal must be as easy as consent, access may not be restricted for refusal, buttons must share size, tone and colour, and the storage period of a refusal must equal that of an acceptance. Scrolling, continued browsing and pre-ticked boxes are invalid. The HDPA re-invoked points C4 and C7 in its 2022 action on news websites.

title: UOOU (Czech Republic), cookies only with consent from 1 January 2022 (amendment to the Electronic Communications Act)
takeaway: The Czech DPA explains that the amendment to Act No. 127/2005 on Electronic Communications, effective 1 January 2022, removed the ambiguity that had let operators read the law as opt-out: website operators may collect visitors' data through cookies only on the basis of demonstrable consent (opt-in), with an exception only for technical cookies necessary for transmission and for providing the service, including security. Consent through pre-set browser settings or a statement that staying on the site means consent is not valid, and the controller must be able to prove consent. Czech-facing sites should present layered information and per-purpose choices.

title: noyb, cookie banner campaign launch: more than 500 draft complaints to websites using unlawful banners
takeaway: noyb sent draft complaints to more than 500 websites across 33 countries, generated with an automated scanner, after finding that 81 percent of scanned banners offered no reject option on the first layer, 73 percent used deceptive colours and contrasts, and 90 percent offered no simple way to withdraw consent, and announced up to 10,000 complaints over 2021. Recipients were given a month to fix their banners before formal complaints. The campaign, later routed through ten data protection authorities, is the origin of many of the national decisions on this page, including the Austrian, Swedish and Belgian ones.

title: noyb, 422 formal GDPR complaints filed against cookie banners after the warning period
takeaway: After the May 2021 warning letters, noyb reported that 42 percent of the flagged violations were remedied within 30 days but 82 percent of companies had not fully stopped violating the GDPR, and filed 422 formal complaints with ten European authorities, plus 36 complaints against major platforms, targeting missing reject buttons, pre-ticked boxes, deceptive colours, absent withdrawal options and unsupported legitimate-interest claims. Roughly half went to the Austrian DPA. Decisions from these complaints continued to arrive in 2025 and 2026, so a banner that passed in 2021 may still be the subject of a pending case.

title: noyb and the Norwegian Consumer Council, complaint against Schibsted's pay or okay model with the Norwegian DPA
takeaway: noyb filed a complaint with Datatilsynet, together with the Norwegian Consumer Council, alleging that Schibsted's requirement that readers either accept tracking for personalised advertising or pay a fee produces consent rates near 99 percent although only a small share of users want to be tracked, so consent is not freely given under the GDPR. noyb states that the Swedish IMY has received at least 56 complaints against Schibsted since the Swedish rollout. The complaint is pending; Nordic publishers should expect the first consent-or-pay decisions under ekomloven section 3-15 and the GDPR to come from this case.

title: ePrivacy Directive 2002/58/EC as amended by Directive 2009/136/EC, Article 5(3) and Article 13
takeaway: Article 5(3) permits the storing of information, or the gaining of access to information already stored, in a user's terminal equipment only with consent given after clear and comprehensive information, with exceptions for transmission of a communication and for storage or access strictly necessary for a service explicitly requested by the user. Article 13(1) requires prior consent for automated calls, fax and email marketing, and Article 13(2) sets the soft opt-in for email marketing of own similar products to existing customers. The rules bind anyone placing cookies, pixels or scripts on EU users' devices, whatever the sender's location. Map every tag against the two exemptions and keep the consent record.

title: General Data Protection Regulation (EU) 2016/679, Articles 4(11), 6, 7 and 25 and Recital 30
takeaway: Article 4(11) defines consent as freely given, specific, informed and unambiguous, shown by a statement or clear affirmative action, and Article 7 adds the burden of proof, separability, and withdrawal as easy as giving consent. Recital 30 names cookie identifiers and IP addresses as identifiers that may make a person identifiable, so tracking data is personal data and Article 6 requires a legal basis for what follows collection. Article 25 requires privacy by design and by default, applied by regulators to default banner settings. Applies from 25 May 2018 to processing in the context of an EU establishment and, under Article 3(2), to controllers elsewhere that offer goods or services to people in the Union or monitor their behaviour there (residence or citizenship alone is not the test); fines reach 20 million euro or 4 per cent of turnover.

title: Digital Services Act, Regulation (EU) 2022/2065, Article 25 (dark patterns), Article 26 (advertising transparency) and Article 28 (minors)
takeaway: Article 25(1) prohibits online platforms from designing or operating interfaces that deceive or manipulate users or materially distort their ability to make free and informed decisions, with Article 25(3) naming repeated choice prompts and prominence tricks as examples and Article 25(2) carving out practices covered by the GDPR or the Unfair Commercial Practices Directive. Article 26 requires each advertisement to show that it is an ad, who paid for it and the main targeting parameters, and bans ads profiled on special-category data. Article 28(2) bans profiling-based ads where the platform is reasonably certain the user is a minor. Applies from 17 February 2024; fines reach 6 per cent of turnover.

title: Digital Markets Act, Regulation (EU) 2022/1925, Article 5(2) (consent for combining and cross-using personal data)
takeaway: Article 5(2) prohibits a gatekeeper from processing third-party data for advertising through its core platform services, combining personal data across its services or with third-party data, cross-using data between services, or signing users in to other services to combine data, unless the user has been presented with a specific choice and has given GDPR-standard consent. A refused or withdrawn consent may be asked for again at most once a year. The obligation binds each designated gatekeeper six months after its designation, which for the first six gatekeepers meant 6 March 2024, with fines up to 10 per cent of worldwide turnover and 20 per cent for repeat infringements. Publishers using gatekeeper advertising products should expect the gatekeeper to surface the consent moment and align their tag configuration with it.

title: EDPB Guidelines 2/2023 on the technical scope of Article 5(3) of the ePrivacy Directive, version 2.0
takeaway: The guidelines set four criteria for Article 5(3): information, whether personal or not; terminal equipment of a user; a connection to a public communications network; and storage of, or gaining access to, that information. Paragraphs 47 to 63 apply them to URL and pixel tracking, local processing whose output is sent to a third party, tracking based on IP address alone, IoT reporting and unique identifiers, and find that each falls within Article 5(3) where the instruction to send information comes from code the entity distributed. Treat server-side tagging, link decoration, fingerprinting and pixel calls as consent events unless an exemption applies. Version 1.0 of 14 November 2023 is superseded.

title: EDPB Guidelines 05/2020 on consent under Regulation 2016/679
takeaway: The guidelines spell out the Article 4(11) and Article 7 conditions and add two positions that shape banners directly: access to a website cannot be conditioned on accepting cookies (a cookie wall does not produce freely given consent, paragraph 39), and scrolling or swiping through a page is not a clear affirmative action (paragraph 86). They also require granular purposes, a documented record, and withdrawal as easy as giving consent. They set the standard the authorities apply to every controller relying on consent, including for the GDPR processing that follows a cookie. Use them as the checklist for banner wording, button design and consent logs. They replace Article 29 Working Party Guidelines WP259 on consent.

title: EDPB Guidelines 03/2022 on deceptive design patterns in social media platform interfaces, version 2.0
takeaway: The guidelines name six families of deceptive design pattern, overloading, skipping, stirring, obstructing, fickle and left in the dark, and assess each against Article 5(1)(a) fairness and transparency, Article 12 transparency, Article 25 data protection by design and default, and the Articles 4(11) and 7 consent conditions. They are written for social media providers but the assessment method transfers to any consent interface, and supervisory authorities cite them in cookie banner decisions. Use the pattern catalogue as an audit list for banner copy, colour contrast, click depth and withdrawal paths, and record the review under Article 5(2) accountability.

title: EDPB Opinion 5/2019 on the interplay between the ePrivacy Directive and the GDPR
takeaway: The opinion holds that where the ePrivacy Directive particularises the GDPR the specific rule prevails, so where Article 5(3) requires consent for storing or accessing information on a device, no other Article 6 GDPR basis can replace it, and the later processing of the personal data collected still needs its own GDPR basis. It also confirms that the GDPR one-stop-shop and consistency mechanism do not extend to ePrivacy enforcement, which stays with the national authority each Member State designates. Adopted under Article 64(2), it states the reading the supervisory authorities apply to every operator. Expect parallel national enforcement of cookie rules without a lead authority, and never justify a tracking cookie on legitimate interest.

title: EDPB Opinion 08/2024 on valid consent in the context of consent or pay models implemented by large online platforms
takeaway: Requested by the Dutch, Norwegian and Hamburg authorities, the opinion finds that in most cases a large online platform offering only a choice between behavioural advertising and a fee will not obtain freely given consent, and that platforms should consider an equivalent alternative without a fee, in particular a free version with advertising that processes less or no personal data (paragraphs 73 to 77). Any fee must not inhibit free choice (paragraph 85), and imbalance of power, lock-in and network effects weigh against validity (paragraphs 99 to 112). Authorities apply its reasoning to publishers. Model any paid alternative against the free, less intrusive option; general EDPB guidelines are in preparation.

title: EDPB Report of the work undertaken by the Cookie Banner Taskforce
takeaway: The report records the positions supervisory authorities share on the noyb banner complaints: a first layer with an accept button but no reject option is non-compliant (paragraphs 6 to 8); pre-ticked boxes do not create consent (paragraphs 9 to 10); a reject option hidden as a small link or outside the banner is insufficient (paragraphs 11 to 14); unreadable button contrast is manifestly misleading (paragraph 18); legitimate interest cannot ground a cookie under Article 5(3) (paragraphs 20 to 25); operators must prove and keep updated the list of essential cookies (paragraph 27); and withdrawal must be as easy as consent (paragraph 34). It sets the common enforcement baseline.

title: EDPB Guidelines 8/2020 on the targeting of social media users, version 2.0
takeaway: The guidelines apply Wirtschaftsakademie and Fashion ID to advertising: a targeter that embeds a social media pixel or plug-in jointly determines the purpose of the collection and transmission with the platform and is a joint controller for those operations, though not for what the platform does afterwards. Where targeting relies on tracking across websites, Article 5(3) consent is the only available basis, legitimate interest is excluded, and the parties need an Article 26 arrangement. They set the standard applied to social media providers and to every advertiser or publisher that installs their tags. Tie every pixel to a consent purpose, document the joint controllership split, and cover the transmission in the privacy notice.

title: EDPB Recommendations 2/2025 on the legal basis for requiring the creation of user accounts on e-commerce websites
takeaway: Adopted on 3 December 2025 for a public consultation that closed on 12 February 2026, the recommendations find that a mandatory account for a one-off purchase is unlikely to pass the necessity test under Article 6(1)(b) (paragraph 23), that Article 6(1)(c) applies only exceptionally (paragraph 47), and that order tracking, loyalty, future purchases and fraud prevention do not meet the Article 6(1)(f) necessity and balancing tests (paragraphs 58 to 75). Consent is not available for a compulsory step, and a guest checkout beside voluntary registration is the most efficient lawful design (paragraph 89). They address e-commerce operators. Remove forced registration from checkout and keep account features opt-in.

title: EDPB-EDPS Joint Opinion 2/2026 on the Digital Omnibus proposal
takeaway: The joint opinion supports a regulatory answer to consent fatigue but warns that moving the terminal equipment rules for personal data into the GDPR while non-personal data stays under the ePrivacy Directive splits one rule across two instruments, creates legal uncertainty and must not lower protection; it welcomes the six-month bar on repeat requests after a refusal in proposed Article 88a(4) and strongly supporting machine-readable preference signals in Article 88b. It asks that the Article 88a(3) exemptions be narrow: audience measurement limited to aggregated data not combined across services, and any contextual advertising exemption clearly delimited. It objects strongly to the proposed narrowing of the definition of personal data and to delegating that definition to Commission implementing acts. It binds no one, but it signals how supervisory authorities will read the amended rules if adopted.

title: EDPB letter on the Commission's draft principles for a voluntary cookie pledge
takeaway: The letter gives the Board's feedback on the Commission's draft cookie pledge principles and records that a voluntary pledge cannot lower the consent standard of Article 5(3) ePrivacy and Articles 4(11) and 7 GDPR, and that principles on advertising business models and consent or pay had to be read with the Board's forthcoming opinion on that subject. It addressed the Commission, not operators. Practitioners meet it as one of the reasons the pledge is understood to have stalled and as an early statement of the positions later formalised in Opinion 08/2024. Treat it as background only; the operative EDPB positions are in Opinion 08/2024 and the Cookie Banner Taskforce report.

title: EDPB and European Commission joint guidelines on the interplay between the Digital Markets Act and the GDPR (draft for consultation)
takeaway: The draft guidelines, endorsed by the EDPB and the Commission on 9 October 2025 and put to consultation until 4 December 2025, explain how a gatekeeper satisfies both the specific choice requirement of Article 5(2) DMA and the GDPR consent conditions when it combines or cross-uses personal data across core platform services, and cover data portability, app distribution and messaging interoperability. They address gatekeepers, with indirect effect on the advertisers and publishers that feed data into gatekeeper advertising systems. Use them to understand the consent flows that gatekeeper products will impose on your integrations. The final adopted version had not been located as of September 2026.

title: EDPB work programme 2026-2027 (consent or pay guidelines in preparation)
takeaway: The work programme adopted on 11 February 2026 (published 12 February) lists guidelines on consent or pay among the guidance the Board will deliver in the 2026-2027 cycle; the programme states no scope, but the expectation is that they extend the reasoning of Opinion 08/2024 beyond large online platforms. It binds no one and contains no rule, but it tells publishers running paid ad-free tiers that a general EDPB position covering their model is coming. Keep any consent or pay implementation aligned with Opinion 08/2024 now, including a free alternative with less intrusive advertising where feasible, and plan for a review when the guidelines are published for consultation.

title: CJEU, Case C-673/17, Bundesverband der Verbraucherzentralen v Planet49 GmbH
takeaway: The Court held that consent under Article 5(3) ePrivacy, read with Article 2(h) of Directive 95/46 and Article 4(11) GDPR, is not validly given by a pre-ticked checkbox the user must deselect, and that this applies whether or not the information stored or accessed is personal data. It also held that the information the operator must give includes the duration of the cookies and whether third parties may have access to them. The ruling binds every operator setting cookies on EU users' devices and is the source of the active opt-in rule. Check that no toggle is preset to on and that the banner discloses lifetimes and third-party recipients.

title: CJEU, Case C-61/19, Orange Romania SA v ANSPDCP
takeaway: The Court held under Articles 4(11) and 6(1)(a) GDPR (and the equivalent Directive 95/46 provisions) that the controller must prove the data subject consented by active behaviour after receiving information in clear and plain language, and that a contract clause recording consent does not prove it where the controller pre-ticked the box, where the terms could mislead the customer about being able to contract without consenting, or where refusing required completing an extra form. The case concerned identity documents in a telecoms contract, but the reasoning applies to any consent flow. Keep the refusal path no longer than the acceptance path and retain evidence of the affirmative act.

title: CJEU, Case C-40/17, Fashion ID GmbH & Co. KG v Verbraucherzentrale NRW eV
takeaway: The Court held that a website operator embedding a third-party social plug-in that causes the visitor's browser to send personal data to the plug-in provider is a joint controller with that provider for the collection and disclosure by transmission, but not for the provider's subsequent processing. The operator must itself provide the information due at collection and, where consent is the basis, obtain it for the collection and transmission it controls. It binds every site that embeds a third-party pixel, plug-in or script that fires before consent. Gate every third-party tag behind consent, name the recipient in the notice, and agree the Article 26 allocation with the vendor.

title: CJEU, Case C-252/21, Meta Platforms and Others v Bundeskartellamt
takeaway: The Grand Chamber held that a competition authority may examine GDPR compliance when assessing abuse of dominance, that personalised advertising which finances a social network is not necessary for the contract under Article 6(1)(b) and cannot be justified as a legitimate interest under Article 6(1)(f) for the data at issue, and that a dominant position does not by itself invalidate consent but is an important factor in judging whether it was freely given, with the burden on the operator. Visiting a website revealing sensitive characteristics does not make that data manifestly public. Do not rely on contract or legitimate interest for off-site tracking data used in ad personalisation.

title: CJEU, Case C-604/22, IAB Europe v Gegevensbeschermingsautoriteit
takeaway: The Court held that the TC String generated under the Transparency and Consent Framework is personal data within Article 4(1) GDPR, because combined with an identifier such as an IP address it allows the user to be identified, and that IAB Europe is a joint controller with its members for the recording of users' consent preferences in the TC String, though not for the later processing by participants unless it influences its purposes and means. It binds the framework operator and every publisher and vendor using the TCF. Treat consent strings as personal data in retention, security and rights handling, and run the current TCF version.

title: CJEU, Case C-654/23, Inteligo Media SA v ANSPDCP (soft opt-in and free accounts)
takeaway: The Court held that an email address collected when a user opens a free account giving access to extra articles and a daily newsletter, on a site whose model steers users to paid subscriptions, is obtained in the context of the sale of a product or service within Article 13(2) ePrivacy, so the newsletter promoting the operator's own similar services may be sent under the soft opt-in provided an opt-out was offered at collection and in every message. Where Article 13(2) governs the communication, the Article 6(1) GDPR conditions do not apply in addition. The case arose from a 9,000 euro Romanian fine. Map freemium sign-ups to the soft opt-in.

title: CJEU, Case C-582/14, Patrick Breyer v Bundesrepublik Deutschland (dynamic IP addresses)
takeaway: The Court held that a dynamic IP address recorded by a website operator is personal data in relation to that operator where it has legal means to obtain from the access provider the additional information needed to identify the visitor, and that national law cannot limit the legitimate interest ground so as to exclude retention of that data to keep the site working and defend it against attacks. It binds every operator logging visitor IP addresses, and Recital 30 GDPR and EDPB Guidelines 2/2023 build on it. Treat IP-based analytics, fraud checks and server logs as personal data processing with a stated legal basis and retention period.

title: Proposal for an ePrivacy Regulation, COM(2017) 10, 2017/0003(COD)
takeaway: Tabled on 10 January 2017 to replace Directive 2002/58/EC with a directly applicable regulation on cookies, browser settings and direct marketing, the proposal reached a Council mandate on 10 February 2021 but never a trilogue agreement. The Commission's 2025 work programme of 11 February 2025 announced its withdrawal as outdated and without foreseeable agreement, the College approved the withdrawal on 16 July 2025, and it was published in the Official Journal on 6 October 2025 as C/2025/5423. It never bound anyone. The ePrivacy Directive remains the operative text and the Digital Omnibus of 19 November 2025 is the successor reform vehicle for terminal equipment rules.

title: Digital Omnibus proposal, COM(2025) 837, 2025/0360(COD): new GDPR Articles 88a and 88b on terminal equipment and machine-readable consent signals
takeaway: The proposal moves the rules on storing and accessing personal data on terminal equipment from Article 5(3) ePrivacy into a new GDPR Article 88a, which keeps consent as the default, exempts transmission, requested services, aggregated first-party audience measurement and security, and bars a fresh consent request for the same purpose for at least six months after a refusal. A new Article 88b obliges controllers to honour automated, machine-readable consent and refusal signals once standards exist, with a six-month grace period, and requires browser providers other than SMEs to offer the feature. As of September 2026 the file remains in committee with no Council general approach and no trilogue.

title: Digital Fairness Act initiative (dark patterns, addictive design, consent fatigue)
takeaway: The initiative follows the Commission's fitness check of EU consumer law and targets dark patterns, addictive design, unfair personalisation, influencer marketing and subscription cancellation, with decision fatigue from complex cookie and tracking choices cited as a pattern to address. A public consultation ran from 17 July to 24 October 2025, and the Commission work programme schedules the legislative proposal for the fourth quarter of 2026. As of September 2026 no proposal has been tabled and nothing binds anyone. Expect a consumer-law layer on top of Article 25 DSA and the GDPR for banner design, and audit interfaces now against the EDPB deceptive design categories.

title: European Commission cookie pledge initiative (draft pledging principles)
takeaway: Announced on 28 March 2023 and developed through round tables and working groups, the pledge set out voluntary principles for signatories: no consent request for strictly necessary cookies, upfront disclosure that content is financed by advertising, clear presentation of the business model and the choices, a less intrusive advertising alternative, fewer repeat consent requests per tracker, no further consent requests after a business model choice, and a one-year non-solicitation period after a refusal. Draft principles were presented on 19 December 2023 with signature planned for April 2024, but the Commission published nothing further after January 2024 and the pledge never launched. Its ideas resurface in the Digital Omnibus six-month rule.

title: European Commission non-compliance decision against Meta under Article 5(2) DMA (consent or pay model), fine of 200 million euro
takeaway: The Commission found that Meta's binary choice between consenting to the combination of personal data for personalised advertising and paying for an ad-free subscription, introduced in November 2023, did not give users the specific choice of a service using less personal data that Article 5(2) DMA requires, and fined Meta 200 million euro for the period from March 2024, when DMA obligations became binding, to November 2024, when a revised model was introduced. Apple was fined 500 million euro in the same package. It binds only Meta, but it is the first EU-level enforcement of consent or pay. Publishers copying the model should offer a less data-intensive free option.

title: Personal Information Protection and Electronic Documents Act (PIPEDA), s. 6.1 and Schedule 1 Principle 4.3
takeaway: PIPEDA requires knowledge and consent for the collection, use and disclosure of personal information (Schedule 1, Principle 4.3), and s. 6.1 makes consent valid only where it is reasonable to expect the individual understands the nature, purpose and consequences of the processing. It binds organisations that collect personal information in the course of commercial activity, including foreign operators with a real and substantial connection to Canada. Treat identifiers set by cookies and tracking pixels as personal information, decide whether express or implied consent fits each purpose, and document that analysis; Bill C-36 would replace Part 1 of PIPEDA if enacted.

title: OPC Guidelines on privacy and online behavioural advertising
takeaway: The Commissioner accepts opt-out consent for online behavioural advertising under PIPEDA only where the practice is explained clearly and outside the privacy policy, the opt-out is offered at or before collection, takes effect immediately and persists, no sensitive information is used, children and child-directed sites are not tracked, and data is destroyed or de-identified promptly. Tracking that a user cannot decline, such as zombie cookies or device fingerprinting, must not be used for advertising. It applies to any organisation tracking Canadian users across sites. Configure banners and ad-preference tools to meet each condition, and treat opt-in as required where a condition cannot be met.

title: OPC, OIPC Alberta and OIPC British Columbia, Guidelines for obtaining meaningful consent
takeaway: The three commissioners set seven principles for consent that is meaningful under PIPEDA and the Alberta and British Columbia PIPAs: emphasise key elements, let individuals control the level of detail, offer clear yes or no options for non-essential collection, be innovative, consider the consumer perspective, make consent dynamic, and be accountable. Express consent is required for sensitive information, for uses outside reasonable expectations, and where a meaningful residual risk of significant harm remains. The guidelines have been applied by the offices since 1 January 2019. Build layered notices and just-in-time prompts into consent flows, and keep records that demonstrate the process meets each principle.

title: Joint investigation into location tracking by the Tim Hortons app (PIPEDA Findings 2022-001)
takeaway: The federal, Quebec, Alberta and British Columbia commissioners found that the app collected granular location data every few minutes while closed, contrary to statements that collection occurred only when the app was open, and that the data was gathered for targeted advertising but never used for that purpose, so consent was invalid and the collection lacked an appropriate purpose. The finding binds the operator and signals the offices' approach to tracking statements generally. The company was told to delete the location data, build a privacy management programme with impact assessments, and report within nine months. Align every tracking statement in a banner or policy with what the code actually does.

title: Bill C-27, Digital Charter Implementation Act, 2022 (Consumer Privacy Protection Act)
takeaway: Bill C-27 would have replaced Part 1 of PIPEDA with the Consumer Privacy Protection Act, adding a statutory consent standard, a business-activities exception, rules for de-identified data, administrative penalties and a tribunal, together with the Artificial Intelligence and Data Act. It died on the Order Paper when Parliament was prorogued on 6 January 2025 after committee study but before third reading. Practitioners still meet references to the CPPA in vendor documentation and privacy programmes. Treat those references as historical and map obligations to PIPEDA as it stands and to Bill C-36, which the government tabled on 15 June 2026 as the successor.

title: Bill C-36, Protecting Privacy and Consumer Data Act
takeaway: Bill C-36 would enact the Protecting Privacy and Consumer Data Act to replace Part 1 of PIPEDA, keeping a meaningful consent standard in plain language with expanded exceptions for business activities, research and de-identification, confirming that de-identified information remains personal information, requiring particular attention to children's information, and creating administrative penalties of up to the greater of $10 million or 3 percent of global revenue, with offences up to the greater of $25 million or 5 percent. It received first reading in the House of Commons on 15 June 2026 and has not progressed further. Track the bill, but change nothing in consent flows until it passes.

title: Act respecting the protection of personal information in the private sector (Law 25 amendments), s. 8.1 and s. 9.1
takeaway: Section 8.1, in force since 22 September 2023, requires an enterprise collecting personal information through technology that can identify, locate or profile a person to inform the person first of that technology and of the means available to activate those functions, which the Commission d'accès à l'information reads as requiring such functions to be off by default and switched on only by the individual. Section 9.1 requires the highest confidentiality settings by default but excludes cookies from that specific rule. The Act binds every enterprise handling Quebec residents' information. Configure analytics, advertising and geolocation trackers as opt-in for Quebec visitors and describe the activation controls in the banner.

title: Commission d'accès à l'information, Lignes directrices 2023-1 sur les critères de validité du consentement
takeaway: The Commission's guidelines set eight criteria for valid consent under the public and private sector Acts: manifest, free, informed, given for specific purposes, granular, understandable, temporary, and presented separately from any other information when requested in writing. Consent is not free where refusal takes disproportionate effort compared with acceptance or where visual emphasis such as colour or font size steers the choice, and implied consent requires a genuine opportunity to refuse. The guidelines bind no one directly but state how the Commission will assess consent in investigations. Design banners with equal accept and refuse paths, one purpose per toggle, and a separate consent request for each tracker category.

title: Lei Geral de Proteção de Dados Pessoais (Law 13.709/2018), Articles 7, 8 and 52
takeaway: Article 7 lists ten legal bases, including consent (item I) and legitimate interest (item IX), and Article 8 requires consent in writing or by another means demonstrating the data subject's will, in a highlighted clause when written, with the burden of proof on the controller and revocation available at any time. Article 52 allows fines of up to 2 percent of revenue in Brazil, capped at R$50,000,000 per infraction, plus daily fines, publication and blocking. It binds any processing of data of individuals located in Brazil or carried out in Brazil. Pair each cookie category with a legal basis, record consent events, and keep refusal as easy as acceptance.

title: ANPD Guia orientativo: Cookies e proteção de dados pessoais
takeaway: The guide classifies cookies as necessary or non-necessary, first or third party, session or persistent, and pairs them with legal bases: consent for non-necessary cookies and legitimate interest for necessary ones, with legitimate interest unsuitable for behavioural profiling and advertising. A first-layer banner must offer a reject option as visible as the accept button and a link to the cookie policy, a second layer must give per-category choices with non-necessary cookies off by default, and pre-ticked boxes, hidden refuse buttons, missing revocation and cookie walls are listed as non-compliant. It is advisory but states how the authority reads the LGPD. Use it as the specification for Brazilian banners.

title: ANPD Guia orientativo: Hipóteses legais de tratamento de dados pessoais, legítimo interesse
takeaway: The guide sets out how the ANPD expects controllers to rely on legitimate interest under Article 7, IX and Article 10 of the LGPD: a documented balancing test covering the legitimacy of the interest, the necessity of the processing, the impact on data subjects and their legitimate expectations, with a model assessment in the annex. Legitimate interest cannot be used for sensitive data and has restricted use in the public sector. It applies to any controller invoking the basis, including for analytics or necessary cookies. Complete and retain a balancing test before setting any cookie without consent, and provide transparency and an objection route for the processing.

title: Resolução CD/ANPD nº 4/2023, Regulamento de dosimetria e aplicação de sanções administrativas
takeaway: The regulation sets the method by which the ANPD calculates the sanctions in Article 52 of the LGPD, classifying infractions as light, medium or serious, applying a percentage of revenue within the 2 percent and R$50,000,000 ceilings, and listing aggravating and mitigating factors such as recurrence, good faith, cooperation and adoption of a compliance programme. It binds every processing agent subject to LGPD sanctions, which became applicable on 1 August 2021. Since the first fine in July 2023 the authority has applied it consistently. Keep evidence of consent design, records of processing and remediation steps to support the mitigating factors if a cookie complaint escalates.

title: Enunciado CD/ANPD nº 1/2023 on the processing of children's and adolescents' personal data
takeaway: The statement interprets Article 14 of the LGPD to allow children's and adolescents' data to be processed under any legal basis in Articles 7 and 11, not only specific parental consent, provided the best interest of the minor prevails and is assessed in each case. It binds the ANPD's own enforcement posture and applies to any controller handling minors' data, including operators of sites and apps used by children. Do not rely on it to run behavioural advertising cookies on child-directed services; document a best-interest assessment for any tracker on such services, and default to no tracking where the assessment is unclear.

title: Privacy Act 1988 (Cth), Australian Privacy Principles 3, 5, 6, 7 and 8 (Compilation No. 103)
takeaway: The compilation in force from 10 June 2025 defines personal information as information about an identified or reasonably identifiable individual, defines consent as express or implied, requires consent to collect sensitive information (APP 3.3), notification at or before collection (APP 5), use and disclosure only for the primary purpose or with consent (APP 6), a simple means of opting out of direct marketing (APP 7) and reasonable steps for overseas disclosures (APP 8).
