It binds APP entities, broadly organisations with annual turnover above $3 million and all health service providers. Map every pixel and cookie to these principles and obtain express consent before any tracker can capture sensitive information.

title: Privacy and Other Legislation Amendment Act 2024 (No. 128, 2024)
takeaway: The first tranche of Privacy Act reform received assent on 10 December 2024. It creates a statutory tort for serious invasions of privacy from 10 June 2025, requires the OAIC to register a Children's Online Privacy Code by 10 December 2026, requires privacy policies to disclose automated decision-making from 10 December 2026, gives the Commissioner infringement and compliance notice powers from 11 December 2024, and adds tiered civil penalties. It binds all APP entities. Update privacy policies for the automated decision-making disclosure before the deadline, and plan for the Children's Code where a service is likely to be accessed by children.

title: OAIC guidance: Tracking pixels and privacy obligations
takeaway: The Commissioner explains that a third-party pixel collects IP address, location, URLs and transaction data and sends it to an advertising platform, engaging APP 1, 3, 5, 6, 7, 8 and 11. Organisations must understand the pixel before deployment, review the provider's terms, run a privacy impact assessment, configure it to collect the minimum, avoid site-wide placement, prevent capture of sensitive information without express opt-in consent, notify users through banners or notices naming the recipients and any overseas transfer, and offer a simple opt-out from targeted advertising. It applies to every APP entity using pixels. Treat the list as a pre-deployment checklist and revisit it at each review cycle.

title: Commissioner-initiated investigations into Medmate Australia and Monash IVF (tracking pixels), [2026] AICmr 40 and 41
takeaway: The Privacy Commissioner determined on 11 June 2026 that a telehealth provider and a fertility provider breached APP 3.3 by collecting sensitive health information through third-party tracking pixels without consent, APP 5.1 by failing to notify, and APP 7.1 by using sensitive information for direct marketing without consent. Monash IVF ran seven pixels from 30 July 2012 to 9 December 2024 and Medmate from April 2021 to 9 December 2024; neither ran a privacy impact assessment, and the argument that data sent straight to a platform was not collected was rejected. The determinations bind the two entities. Remove or gate pixels on any page revealing a health topic.

title: OAIC guidance: Direct marketing (APP 7)
takeaway: The guidance confirms that APP 7 covers targeted online marketing whenever personal information is used or disclosed to deliver it, alongside email and post, while communications covered by the Spam Act 2003 and the Do Not Call Register Act 2006 sit outside APP 7. Organisations must provide a simple means of opting out, draw attention to it in each communication where practicable, and stop using or disclosing the information within a reasonable period after a request. It applies to organisations covered by the Privacy Act. Link the advertising toggle in the banner to a working suppression mechanism so that an opt-out from targeted advertising is honoured across ad platforms.

title: OAIC exposure draft of the Children's Online Privacy Code
takeaway: The draft Code, released on 31 March 2026 for consultation to 5 June 2026, would apply to APP entities providing social media, relevant electronic services or designated internet services likely to be accessed by children, other than health services. It requires collection, use and disclosure to be consistent with the child's best interests, permits direct marketing to children only with consent, in the child's best interests and from information collected directly from the child, and requires age-appropriate notices and a deletion right. The Act requires registration by 10 December 2026. Inventory trackers on child-accessible services now and plan to disable advertising and profiling cookies for those audiences.

title: Exposure draft, Privacy Amendment (Personal Data Protection) Bill 2026 (tranche 2 reforms)
takeaway: The Attorney-General's Department released the tranche 2 exposure draft on 31 August 2026 with consultation closing on 18 September 2026. It would define consent as voluntary, informed, current, specific and unambiguous, extend collection to information generated or inferred, confirm that IP addresses, device identifiers and cookie IDs are personal information where reasonably linkable, make precise geolocation tracking data sensitive, add a fair and reasonable test weighing the child's best interests, require consent before trading personal information, and require an opt-out from targeted online behavioural advertising with an ad-free alternative where a service relies on marketing revenue. It is not law. Model banner changes now against the proposed standard.

title: ACCC Digital advertising services inquiry, final report
takeaway: The competition regulator's final report, released on 28 September 2021, found competition in ad tech ineffective because of opacity across the supply chain and the data advantage of the largest intermediary, and made six recommendations, including that the leading provider explain publicly how it uses first-party data in ad tech, sector-specific rules allowing data separation or access remedies, and transparency standards backed by mandatory rules if voluntary measures fail. It binds no one but frames how the ACCC assesses consent and data flows in advertising, complementing its 2019 platforms inquiry call for opt-in consent. Expect Australian regulators to read consent strings and data-sharing settings as competition evidence too.

title: Act on the Protection of Personal Information (APPI), Article 2(7) and Article 31 (personally referable information)
takeaway: Since the 2020 amendment took effect on 1 April 2022, Article 31 prohibits a business from providing personally referable information, such as cookie identifiers and browsing history that do not identify a person on their own, to a third party expected to link it to an identified individual, unless the business has confirmed that the recipient obtained the individual's consent and recorded that confirmation. The consolidated English text is current to 1 April 2023. It binds every business handling personal information, including foreign operators serving Japanese users. Where a pixel or SDK sends identifiers to an advertising platform that matches them to accounts, verify and record the platform's consent first.

title: PPC Guidelines on the Act on the Protection of Personal Information (General Rules edition), section 2-8 on personally referable information
takeaway: The Commission's general guidelines, first issued in November 2016 and last partially revised in June 2026, define personally referable information as information that does not identify an individual by itself but can identify one when combined with other data, and explain the Article 31 confirmation and record-keeping duties when such information is provided to a third party that will treat it as personal data. They bind no one directly but state the standard the Commission applies in supervision. Use section 2-8 to decide, for each tag on the site, whether the recipient will link the identifier to a person and therefore whether the recipient's consent must be confirmed first.

title: PPC Guidelines Q&A on the APPI (updated edition)
takeaway: The Commission's consolidated Q&A, last updated on 1 July 2025, answers practical questions under the guidelines, including how cookies and advertising identifiers are treated, when browsing data becomes personally referable information, what form the recipient's consent must take under Article 31, and how the providing business may confirm and record that consent. It binds no one but reflects the Commission's supervisory reading and is cited in inspections. Keep the Q&A numbers for cookies and Article 31 in the tag governance file, and use its examples to set the consent wording that advertising partners must show before matching identifiers to user accounts.

title: Telecommunications Business Act, Article 27-12 (external transmission rule) and MIC guidance
takeaway: The 2022 amendment to the Telecommunications Business Act, in force from 16 June 2023, requires operators of messaging services, social networks, search services and websites delivering news or information to inform users before a browser or app sends user information to an external party, by notice or easily accessible publication, by consent, or by an opt-out. The disclosure must state the information sent, the recipient and the purpose of use. Information necessary to deliver the service and identifiers sent to the operator itself are exempt; e-commerce sites and personal blogs are outside scope. Publish an external transmission page listing every third-party tag, recipient and purpose, linked from the banner.

title: Personal Information Protection Act (PIPA), as amended with effect from 15 September 2023
takeaway: The amended Act, in force from 15 September 2023, unifies the rules for online service providers and other controllers, requires consent to collect personal information unless another basis applies, requires separate consent for marketing and third-party provision, requires the privacy policy to describe the installation, operation and refusal of automatic collection devices such as cookies, adds a right to refuse automated decisions, and raises the penalty surcharge to up to 3 percent of total related sales. It binds domestic and foreign operators processing Korean residents' data. Provide granular opt-in consent for behavioural advertising cookies, keep the cookie section of the privacy policy current, and expect PIPC audits of consent screens.

title: PIPC and KCC Guideline on personal information protection in online customised advertising (behavioural information)
takeaway: The guideline treats behavioural information collected through cookies and advertising identifiers as protected data, requires advertising businesses and website operators to disclose the items collected, the collection method, the purpose, the retention period and how users can control the processing, prohibits collection of sensitive behavioural information without consent, requires separate treatment of children under 14, and calls for an accessible opt-out. It is guidance and binds no one directly, but the Commission applied its standard in the September 2022 sanctions against Google and Meta. In January 2024 the Commission announced a policy plan to revise it. Publish a behavioural information notice and an opt-out that works across advertising partners.

title: PIPC sanctions Google and Meta for collecting behavioural information without consent
takeaway: The Commission imposed penalty surcharges of KRW 69.2 billion on Google and KRW 30.8 billion on Meta for collecting users' behavioural information from third-party websites and apps and using it for customised advertising without clearly informing users or obtaining consent, finding that Google hid the setting behind a default-on option and that Meta buried the disclosure in its terms. The decision binds the two companies and set the largest surcharges under the Act at the time. Corrective orders required an easy, clear consent screen for third-party behavioural data. Treat any cross-site behavioural data flow into Korean advertising accounts as requiring separate, explicit consent presented outside the terms of service.

title: PIPC sanctions Meta for refusing service to users who declined behavioural data collection
takeaway: The Commission fined Meta KRW 660 million, for making acceptance of behavioural information collection for customised advertising a condition of using the service, contrary to the rule that a controller must not refuse a service because a user declines to consent to processing beyond what is necessary for the service. The decision binds the company and states the Commission's position that access to a social network cannot be conditioned on advertising consent. Do not deploy cookie walls or consent-or-leave designs for Korean users, and keep the service usable when advertising consent is withheld.

title: Personal Information Protection Law (PIPL), Articles 13, 14, 24 and 66
takeaway: Article 13 lists the lawful bases, with consent first and no legitimate-interest basis, and Article 14 requires consent given voluntarily and explicitly on the basis of full information, refreshed when purpose, method or categories change. Article 24 requires that information push or commercial marketing based on automated decision-making be accompanied by an option not targeted at personal characteristics or a convenient way to refuse, and Article 66 allows fines up to RMB 50 million or 5 percent of the prior year's turnover for serious violations. It binds handlers in China and foreign handlers targeting individuals in China. Offer a visible non-personalised mode and a one-step refusal of personalised advertising.

title: Cybersecurity Law, Article 22 and Article 41
takeaway: Article 22 requires providers of network products and services with functions that collect user information to tell users and obtain their consent, and Article 41 requires network operators to collect and use personal information lawfully, properly and only as necessary, to publish their collection and use rules, to state purpose, method and scope, and to obtain consent. The law, in force since 1 June 2017, binds network operators in China and is the basis on which the Cyberspace Administration inspects apps and websites for undisclosed collection. Keep a published collection rule for every site and SDK and make sure the banner text matches the collection actually performed.

title: Provisions on the Management of Algorithmic Recommendations in Internet Information Services, Articles 17, 18 and 21
takeaway: The provisions, in force from 1 March 2022, require algorithmic recommendation providers to offer users an option not targeted at their personal characteristics or a convenient way to turn the recommendation service off, to let users select or delete the user tags used for recommendations, to protect minors from harmful or addictive content, and not to use algorithms to apply unreasonable differential prices or transaction conditions based on user characteristics. They bind providers of algorithmic recommendation services to users in China. Implement a tag management screen and a global personalisation switch, and record the state of the switch with the same rigour as cookie consent.

title: Regulations on Network Data Security Management (State Council Decree 790), Articles 21, 22 and 42
takeaway: Published on 30 September 2024 and in force from 1 January 2025, the regulations require network data handlers to publish processing rules in a prominent place, to collect only what is necessary, to obtain separate consent for sensitive information and parental consent for children under 14, and not to repeat a consent request after refusal. Article 42 requires platform providers that push information by automated decision-making to offer an easy-to-understand, easy-to-reach switch to turn off personalised recommendation and to let users delete their tags. They bind network data handlers processing Chinese individuals' data. Remove repeated consent prompts and place the personalisation switch within the first layer of settings.

title: GB/T 35273-2020, Information security technology: Personal information security specification
takeaway: The recommended national standard, published on 6 March 2020 and implemented on 1 October 2020, sets the detailed practice that regulators and app stores use to assess personal information handling: separate consent for each business function, no bundling of functions, personalised display marked as such with a way to opt out, restraints on third-party SDK data collection with contractual and technical controls, and privacy policy templates. It is voluntary in form but is the reference in CAC, MIIT and TC260 app assessments. Audit every embedded SDK against the standard's third-party access clauses and label personalised advertising content as required.

title: Measures for Determining Illegal Collection and Use of Personal Information by Apps (App违法违规收集使用个人信息行为认定方法)
takeaway: Issued jointly by the CAC, MIIT, Ministry of Public Security and SAMR, the measures list six categories of violation used in app enforcement: no privacy policy or one not shown at first launch or reachable within four clicks, unclear purpose, method and scope, collection before or after refusal of consent including default consent and inducement, collection of unnecessary data or refusal of service when non-essential data is declined, unauthorised sharing with third parties through embedded code or servers, and missing deletion, correction and complaint channels. They bind app operators in China and drive the CAC's periodic public naming of apps. Test the app against each category before release.

title: Provisions on the Scope of Necessary Personal Information for Common Types of Mobile Apps
takeaway: Issued on 22 March 2021 and effective from 1 May 2021, the provisions define for 39 common app types the personal information necessary for basic functions, from location for navigation to phone number for social platforms, and state that an app must not refuse basic services because a user declines to provide non-necessary personal information; news, browser and utility apps need no personal information for basic use. They bind app operators and are enforced through CAC and MIIT app checks. Map every SDK and tracker to the necessary-information list for the app's category and keep advertising and analytics collection strictly optional.

title: Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, sections 6, 9 and the Schedule
takeaway: The Act, assented to on 11 August 2023, requires consent that is free, specific, informed, unconditional and unambiguous with a clear affirmative action, limited to necessary data and withdrawable with the same ease (section 6), manageable through a registered Consent Manager. Section 9 requires verifiable parental consent for anyone under 18 and prohibits tracking, behavioural monitoring and targeted advertising directed at children; the Schedule sets penalties up to INR 250 crore for security failures and INR 200 crore for children's obligations. It binds data fiduciaries processing digital personal data in India or serving India, phased in under the 2025 Rules. Remove behavioural tracking from services used by minors.

title: Digital Personal Data Protection Rules, 2025 (consent notice, Consent Managers, verifiable parental consent, phased commencement)
takeaway: The Rules, notified on 13 November 2025, bring the Act into force in phases: the Data Protection Board provisions immediately, the Consent Manager framework after twelve months on 13 November 2026, and the remaining obligations, including consent notices, children's verifiable consent and breach notification, after eighteen months on 13 May 2027. They prescribe the content of a consent notice, the registration conditions for Consent Managers, and the methods for verifying a parent's identity and age. They bind every data fiduciary within the Act's scope. Schedule the consent banner rebuild and children's age-assurance design for completion before 13 May 2027 and plan integration with registered Consent Managers.

title: Personal Data Protection Act 2012, Parts 4 and 9A (consent, deemed consent by notification, legitimate interests, financial penalties)
takeaway: The Act requires consent, or deemed consent, before collecting, using or disclosing personal data, and the 2020 amendments in force from 1 February 2021 added deemed consent by notification, available only after an assessment shows no likely adverse effect and a reasonable opt-out period is given, and a legitimate interests exception that cannot be used for direct marketing. Financial penalties of up to 10 percent of annual turnover in Singapore or S$1 million, whichever is higher, apply from 1 October 2022. It binds organisations processing data in Singapore. Use deemed consent by notification only for low-risk cookies with a documented assessment, and obtain express consent for behavioural advertising.

title: PDPC Advisory Guidelines on the PDPA for Selected Topics, chapter on online activities (cookies and behavioural targeting)
takeaway: The Commission's guidelines state that consent is not required for cookies needed to provide the service the user requested, that deemed consent may cover other cookies where the user voluntarily provides data with knowledge of the purpose, that behavioural targeting using personal data requires consent with a clear explanation of the purpose, and that IP addresses and device identifiers are personal data when they can identify an individual alone or with other data. They bind no one directly but state how the Commission assesses complaints. Classify each cookie as necessary, deemed-consent or express-consent, keep a written justification, and present advertising cookies as an opt-in choice.

title: Personal Data Protection Act B.E. 2562 (2019), sections 19, 23 and 82 to 90
takeaway: The Act, fully in force since 1 June 2022 after two deferrals, requires consent under section 19 to be explicit, in writing or electronic form, requested separately from other matters in a clear and accessible format without deceptive conditions, and withdrawable as easily as it was given, and section 23 requires a privacy notice before or at collection. Administrative fines reach THB 5 million and criminal penalties include imprisonment of up to one year for certain sensitive-data offences. It binds controllers in Thailand and foreign controllers offering goods or services to people in Thailand. Use a separate, granular cookie consent screen and keep necessary cookies outside the consent request.

title: Protection of Personal Information Act 4 of 2013 (POPIA), sections 11, 18, 69 and 107 to 109
takeaway: POPIA commenced on 1 July 2020 with a grace period ending 30 June 2021. Section 11 requires a lawful basis such as consent or legitimate interest, section 18 requires notification of the purpose and source of collection, and section 69 prohibits direct marketing by electronic communication unless the data subject has consented or is an existing customer marketed with similar products, with an opt-out in every message; the Information Regulator may impose administrative fines of up to R10 million. The Act binds responsible parties domiciled in South Africa or using means there. Treat advertising cookies that feed electronic direct marketing as needing opt-in consent, and document legitimate-interest reliance for analytics.

title: Saudi Arabia Personal Data Protection Law (Royal Decree M/19 as amended by M/148) and Implementing Regulations
takeaway: The PDPL, amended in March 2023 and in force from 14 September 2023 with a compliance grace period to 14 September 2024, requires a lawful basis for processing, consent that can be withdrawn at any time, and a published privacy policy, and its Implementing Regulations allow direct marketing only with consent or to existing customers with an opt-out in every message. Fines reach SAR 5 million and double for repeat violations, with the Saudi Data and Artificial Intelligence Authority supervising, and foreign controllers processing residents' data are bound. Treat advertising cookies as consent-based and include a marketing opt-out in the banner's second layer.

title: UAE Federal Decree-Law No. 45 of 2021 on the Protection of Personal Data
takeaway: The federal PDPL, effective 2 January 2022, requires consent that is clear, specific, informed and withdrawable unless another basis applies, and gives data subjects a right to object to processing for direct marketing and to automated decision-making, with the UAE Data Office as regulator. It applies to controllers in the UAE outside the financial free zones, which run their own regimes, and to foreign controllers processing UAE residents' data. Executive regulations that would set detailed consent mechanics and penalties have not been issued, so obligations are applied from the law's text. Run advertising cookies on opt-in consent and offer an objection route for profiling.

title: Israel Protection of Privacy Law 5741-1981 as amended by Amendment 13
takeaway: Amendment 13, in force from 14 August 2025, modernises the 1981 law by widening the definitions of personal and sensitive data, requiring that a request for information state whether provision is mandatory, the purposes, recipients and rights, giving the Privacy Protection Authority powers to audit, order and impose administrative fines, and applying the law to foreign entities processing Israeli residents' data. Direct marketing databases remain subject to the database registration and opt-out rules. Practitioners should present cookie notices in Hebrew with the statutory disclosure items and maintain an easy opt-out from direct marketing profiles built from tracking data.

title: Argentina Personal Data Protection Law 25.326, Articles 5, 6 and 27
takeaway: Law 25.326 requires free, express and informed consent, in writing or by an equivalent means, before personal data is processed unless an exception applies (Article 5), requires notice of purpose and recipients (Article 6), and lets any person opt out of processing for advertising at any time and without cost (Article 27). The Agency of Access to Public Information enforces it with fines that remain low under the current scale; a replacement bill with turnover-based fines has been pending since 2023. It binds controllers in Argentina and those using means there. Present advertising cookies as opt-in and provide a no-cost objection route for marketing profiles.

title: Mexico Ley Federal de Protección de Datos Personales en Posesión de los Particulares (2025)
takeaway: The new federal law, published on 20 March 2025 and in force from 21 March 2025, replaces the 2010 statute, moves supervision from INAI to the Secretaría Anticorrupción y Buen Gobierno, keeps tacit consent for non-sensitive data where the privacy notice is provided and the person does not object, requires express consent for sensitive and financial data (written for sensitive data), and subjects transfers to third parties to the consent form that applies to the data concerned, with the statutory exceptions for group companies, legal requirements and contracts in the person's interest. The privacy notice must be available before collection, and the regulations continue to require disclosure of cookies, web beacons and similar technologies and how to disable them. It binds private-sector controllers in Mexico. Keep the cookie disclosure in the notice and offer an objection route.

title: Colombia Statutory Law 1581 of 2012 and Decree 1377 of 2013 (prior, express and informed authorisation)
takeaway: Law 1581 requires prior, express and informed authorisation from the data subject before personal data is collected, and Decree 1377 allows that authorisation to be given by unequivocal conduct but never by silence, with the controller bearing the burden of proof. The Superintendencia de Industria y Comercio enforces the law and has sanctioned operators for collecting data through websites without valid authorisation, with fines of up to 2,000 monthly minimum wages. It binds controllers in Colombia and foreign controllers subject to Colombian law by treaty. Use an affirmative consent action for non-essential cookies, record the authorisation, and publish the treatment policy the law requires.

title: Kenya Data Protection Act 2019 and Data Protection (General) Regulations 2021 (direct marketing)
takeaway: The Act, in force from 25 November 2019, requires a lawful basis including consent that is express, unequivocal, free, specific and informed, and the General Regulations of 2021 permit direct marketing only with consent or to existing customers with an opt-out, and require controllers to use the least intrusive means of profiling. The Office of the Data Protection Commissioner enforces with penalties of up to KES 5 million or 1 percent of annual turnover and has issued determinations against operators for unsolicited marketing. It binds controllers in Kenya and those processing Kenyan residents' data. Treat advertising cookies as consent-based and honour marketing opt-outs across channels.

title: Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023 and NDPC General Application and Implementation Directive 2025
takeaway: The Act, signed on 12 June 2023, replaces the 2019 Regulation, requires consent that is freely given, specific, informed and unambiguous with the controller bearing the burden of proof, gives a right to object to direct marketing, and empowers the Nigeria Data Protection Commission to impose penalties of up to the greater of NGN 10 million and 2 per cent of annual gross revenue for controllers of major importance (NGN 2 million or 2 per cent for others). The Commission's General Application and Implementation Directive of 2025 adds detailed rules on consent design, cookie notices and privacy policies. It binds controllers in Nigeria and foreign controllers processing Nigerians' data. Deploy a consent banner with a documented consent log and a marketing objection route.

title: Indonesia Law No. 27 of 2022 on Personal Data Protection
takeaway: The law, enacted on 17 October 2022 with a two-year transition that ended on 17 October 2024, requires explicit consent, in writing or recorded form, as the primary basis for processing, requires that a consent request be presented clearly and separately from other matters and be withdrawable, and gives data subjects rights to object to profiling and automated decisions, with administrative fines of up to 2 percent of annual revenue. A dedicated supervisory authority and implementing regulations were still being established after the transition ended. It binds controllers in Indonesia and foreign controllers whose processing has legal effect there. Run advertising and analytics cookies on explicit, separately presented consent.

title: Vietnam Personal Data Protection Law (Law 91/2025/QH15), successor to Decree 13/2023/ND-CP
takeaway: The Law, passed on 26 June 2025 and in force from 1 January 2026, carries forward the consent standard of Decree 13/2023/ND-CP (in force from 1 July 2023): consent must be voluntary, specific, informed and given per purpose, and silence is not consent. It adds fines of up to 5 percent of the previous year's revenue for unlawful cross-border transfers and up to ten times the revenue gained from unlawful sale of personal data, and requires controllers to give users a way to refuse tracking and personalised advertising. It binds domestic and foreign controllers processing Vietnamese residents' data. Present cookie consent per purpose and provide a working tracking opt-out.

title: Philippines Data Privacy Act of 2012 (Republic Act 10173) and NPC guidelines on consent
takeaway: The Act defines consent as a freely given, specific, informed indication of will evidenced by written, electronic or recorded means, requires a privacy notice before collection, and gives data subjects a right to object to processing for direct marketing and profiling. The National Privacy Commission's guidelines on consent state that consent may not be bundled, that pre-ticked boxes and silence are not consent, and that withdrawal must be as easy as giving it, and the Commission has ordered operators to fix non-compliant consent interfaces. It binds controllers in the Philippines and those processing Filipino residents' data. Use an affirmative cookie consent action and an accessible withdrawal control.

title: IAB Europe Transparency and Consent Framework v2.2
takeaway: TCF v2.2 launched on 16 May 2023 and removed legitimate interest as a legal basis for advertising and content personalisation purposes 3 to 6, replaced legal text with plain-language purpose descriptions, required vendors to declare data categories and retention periods, and obliged CMPs to show the total number of vendors on the first layer and to offer an easy route to withdrawal. It binds registered CMPs, vendors and publishers by contract, with switch-over required by 20 November 2023; it is an industry standard, not law, though the Belgian APD and the courts assessed its predecessor. TCF v2.3 of 19 June 2025 supersedes it by making the disclosed vendors segment mandatory.

title: IAB Europe TCF Policies (current version 2026-05-29.5.0.b)
takeaway: The TCF Policies are the contractual rulebook behind the TC String, defining purposes, features and legal bases and setting CMP, vendor and publisher obligations. CMPs must generate consent signals only on a clear affirmative action, resolve conflicting signals before transmission, implement publisher restrictions and resurface the interface when IAB Europe notifies material policy changes; vendors must respect signals in real time and stop processing if a signal cannot be verified; publishers may use only compliant CMPs and vendors. The Policies bind registered participants by contract and are not law, although the Belgian APD and the Brussels Market Court examined earlier versions; check which version your CMP implements.

title: IAB Europe TCF v2.3 and the mandatory disclosed vendors segment
takeaway: TCF v2.3, released on 19 June 2025, makes the disclosedVendors segment of the TC String mandatory so that a vendor can tell whether it was shown to the user or whether the user objected. CMPs had to update by 28 February 2026 without re-surfacing the interface; vendors must read and act on the segment from 1 March 2026, after which a new TC String without it is invalid. TC Strings created before the deadline remain valid until users refresh their choices. The change binds TCF-registered CMPs and vendors by contract, not law; confirm that your CMP's TC Strings carry the segment and that each vendor's ID bit is set.

title: IAB Tech Lab TCF v2 technical specifications and implementation guidelines
takeaway: IAB Tech Lab maintains the TCF v2 technical specifications: the TC String format with its core, disclosed vendors and publisher TC segments, the CMP API through which vendors read signals, and the Global Vendor List (version 3 since v2.2). The implementation guidelines, last updated in May 2023, record the v2.2 changes (revised purpose names, retention periods, no legitimate interest for purposes 3 to 6, data categories, localised policy URLs) and the v2.3 mandatory disclosed vendor segment. They bind participants through the TCF Policies and are not law. Use them to test that your CMP exposes the API correctly and that TC Strings decode to the choices actually made.

title: IAB Europe TCF compliance programmes and CMP validation
takeaway: IAB Europe validates every CMP before it receives a CMP ID and a place on the CMP List, covering the interface and technical operation on web, mobile and CTV, and vets vendors through a questionnaire before Global Vendor List listing. Live installations are monitored: TC String tampering brings immediate suspension of at least four weeks and permanent suspension on a fourth offence within twelve months, and other policy breaches allow 10 business days (5 to 20 for vendors) to remedy before suspension. The programme binds registered participants by contract, not law. Run the public CMP Validator browser extension, available since May 2023, against your own deployments before an audit does.

title: Brussels Market Court judgment of 7 January 2026 annulling the TCF action plan validation
takeaway: The Market Court annulled the APD decision of 11 January 2023 validating IAB Europe's TCF action plan, finding that the APD had built on a decision already found unlawful, had assumed a joint controllership extending to downstream OpenRTB processing that the May 2025 judgment rejected, and had not heard IAB Europe on the intervening CJEU developments. The APD must reassess the plan on the narrower TC String scope after giving IAB Europe the opportunity to take position. The action plan measures already built into TCF v2.2 (consent only for advertising purposes, clearer disclosures, vendor transparency) stay in place, and the 1 March 2026 TCF v2.3 deadline was unaffected.

title: IAB Tech Lab Global Privacy Platform (GPP) and the US National section
takeaway: The Global Privacy Platform is IAB Tech Lab's container for consent and opt-out signals across jurisdictions: the GPP string (specification 1.0 of 28 September 2022, CMP API 1.1 of June 2023) carries sections for IAB Europe TCF, IAB Canada TCF, the US National string (section ID 7, defined by the MSPA US National Technical Specification, version 2.0 in October 2024) and individual US state strings, and records whether a Global Privacy Control signal was received. It is a technical standard adopted by contract and by ad exchanges, not law. Publishers selling programmatic inventory to US or Canadian audiences should emit GPP in place of the deprecated US Privacy String.

title: IAB Multi-State Privacy Agreement (MSPA), Fifth Amended and Restated
takeaway: The MSPA is a springing contract among signatories that governs personal information flows for selecting and delivering digital advertising under US state privacy laws; the Fifth Amended and Restated version took effect on 4 June 2026, after a March 2026 revision prompted by California's Healthline and Honda enforcement actions. First parties operate in either Opt-Out Option Mode or Service Provider Mode, and downstream participants must read and honour signals and verify that counterparties are signatories. The National Approach lets a signatory treat every user as a resident of all covered states. It is a private contract, not law; publishers using it work with the GPP US National string.

title: IAB CCPA Compliance Framework US Privacy String (deprecated)
takeaway: The US Privacy String of the IAB CCPA Compliance Framework encoded a single California do-not-sell choice for the advertising supply chain. IAB Tech Lab stopped maintaining it and set a deprecation date of 31 January 2024, extended from 30 September 2023, because only the Global Privacy Platform can carry the signals required by the Virginia, Colorado, Connecticut and Utah laws that took effect in 2023. It never had legal force. Superseded: replace any remaining usprivacy implementation with GPP section strings, and check that ad partners no longer read the old field as the source of truth.

title: W3C Global Privacy Control (GPC) specification, Working Draft
takeaway: The Global Privacy Control specification, a W3C Working Draft of 17 September 2026 from the Privacy Working Group (First Public Working Draft 21 November 2024), defines a Sec-GPC request header with the value 1, a navigator.globalPrivacyControl boolean, and an optional /.well-known/gpc.json resource by which a site declares that it honours the signal. The signal expresses a request not to sell or share personal data and has legal effect only where a law gives it one; the draft notes that at least four US states recognise it. A draft is not law; read the header and the DOM property and treat them as opt-out requests wherever a state law applies.

title: Global Privacy Control reference site and adoption record (globalprivacycontrol.org)
takeaway: The GPC reference site records the signal's origin and adoption: native support in Brave, DuckDuckGo and Firefox and in browser extensions, adoption as a W3C Privacy Working Group work item in November 2024, and, as of 15 January 2025, guidance from California, Colorado, Connecticut and New Jersey treating GPC as a binding opt-out, with eight further state laws permitting opt-outs through universal mechanisms. It cites the California CCPA regulations' requirement to honour user-enabled global privacy controls. The site is maintained by the signal's proponents and is not law. Use it to track which browsers send the signal and which states enforce it.

title: Connecticut Attorney General advisory on opt-out preference signals
takeaway: The Connecticut Attorney General advised that from 1 January 2025 controllers under the Connecticut Data Privacy Act must treat browser-based opt-out preference signals, in practice Global Privacy Control, as binding opt-out requests for the sale of personal data and targeted advertising, including where the signal conflicts with an earlier choice or loyalty programme membership. Entities such as HIPAA-regulated healthcare providers are exempt. The advisory summarises statutory duties; the statute is what binds. Implement GPC recognition, document it in the privacy notice, and expect scrutiny: Connecticut, California and Colorado announced a joint investigative privacy sweep in 2025.

title: California AB 566, the Opt Me Out Act (browser opt-out preference signal)
takeaway: AB 566, signed on 8 October 2025, amends the CCPA to require a business that develops or maintains a web browser to include a setting that lets a consumer send an opt-out preference signal to every business, easy to use and configure, with an explanation of how the signal works and its intended effect. It operates from 1 January 2027, with a safe harbour for compliant browser makers when a website fails to honour the signal, and the California Privacy Protection Agency may adopt regulations. It binds browser developers; businesses already must honour such signals under the CCPA regulations, so expect more signals from 2027.

title: Google consent mode v2 requirement for EEA traffic
takeaway: Consent mode v2 adds the ad_user_data and ad_personalization parameters to ad_storage and analytics_storage, and Google requires the signals for EEA traffic under its EU user consent policy: from early March 2024 only end users outside the EEA are included in audiences shared with linked advertising products unless the signals are sent, and remarketing and personalisation features stop working for the affected traffic. Default states must be denied before the user acts and updated afterwards; basic mode holds tags until consent, advanced mode sends cookieless pings. It is a platform policy, not law; a CMP satisfies it by mapping its analytics category to analytics_storage and its advertising category to ad_storage, ad_user_data and ad_personalization, provided valid consent is collected where the law requires it and the tags actually respect the signals; the cookieless pings of advanced mode are a platform feature, not a legal exemption.

title: Google EU user consent policy
takeaway: Google's EU user consent policy requires anyone using Google advertising products with end users in the EEA, the UK and Switzerland (Switzerland added on 31 July 2024) to obtain legally valid consent for cookies or other local storage where legally required and for the use of personal data for ad personalisation, to identify every party receiving data, to keep consent records and to tell users how to revoke. Publishers must use a Google-certified CMP and advertisers with EEA traffic must send verified consent signals through TCF or consent mode. It is a contractual policy, not law, but it tracks the ePrivacy Directive and GDPR consent tests.

title: Google certified CMP requirement for ads in the EEA, UK and Switzerland
takeaway: From 16 January 2024 publishers serving personalised ads through AdSense, Ad Manager or AdMob to users in the EEA and UK must use a Google-certified CMP integrated with IAB Europe's TCF; Switzerland followed on 31 July 2024 and CTV inventory had an extension to July 2025. Traffic without a certified CMP is eligible only for non-personalised or limited ads. Certified CMPs must support Google's Additional Consent specification for non-TCF vendors, recertify annually and, since 4 October 2024, pass a check on TC String storage and retention (TCF policy check 30). Google states that certification does not check full TCF or legal compliance, so it is not a compliance opinion.

title: Google Privacy Sandbox: a new path for Privacy Sandbox on the web (third-party cookie reversal)
takeaway: On 22 July 2024 Google abandoned its plan to deprecate third-party cookies in Chrome and said it would instead introduce a browser-level choice that users could adjust at any time, after consultation with the UK Competition and Markets Authority and the Information Commissioner's Office. It committed to keep investing in the Privacy Sandbox APIs and to add IP Protection to Incognito. The post is a vendor announcement with no legal force, but it ended the assumption that consent for third-party cookies would become moot. Superseded by the 22 April 2025 decision not to introduce a standalone prompt and the 17 October 2025 retirement of most Sandbox APIs.

title: Google Privacy Sandbox: next steps for Privacy Sandbox and tracking protections in Chrome
takeaway: On 22 April 2025 Google confirmed that Chrome will not roll out a new standalone prompt for third-party cookies; users keep the existing choice in Chrome's Privacy and Security settings, and Incognito continues to block third-party cookies by default. Google also committed to launch IP Protection in Incognito in the third quarter of 2025 and to publish an updated roadmap for the Sandbox APIs. It is a vendor decision, not law. Third-party cookies therefore remain readable in Chrome for most users, and the consent banner remains the operative control over them under the ePrivacy rules.

title: Google Privacy Sandbox: update on plans for Privacy Sandbox technologies (API retirement)
takeaway: On 17 October 2025 Google announced the retirement of thirteen Privacy Sandbox technologies, including the Topics API, Protected Audience, Attribution Reporting, Private Aggregation and Shared Storage, SelectURL, Related Website Sets, IP Protection, On-Device Personalization, Protected App Signals and the SDK Runtime, to be phased out through the normal Chrome and Android processes without fixed dates. CHIPS and FedCM continue, and Google will pursue an interoperable attribution standard at the W3C. Google keeps its current approach to third-party cookie choice in Chrome. It is a vendor announcement, not law; remove Sandbox-specific purposes from consent flows once the APIs stop shipping.

title: Apple App Tracking Transparency requirement (iOS 14.5)
takeaway: Since 26 April 2021, with iOS 14.5, iPadOS 14.5 and tvOS 14.5, apps must ask permission through the AppTrackingTransparency framework before tracking users or reading the advertising identifier; without permission the IDFA is all zeros and tracking is prohibited. Tracking means linking app data with data from other companies' apps, websites or offline properties for targeted advertising or measurement, or sharing it with data brokers; on-device linking and fraud prevention are excluded. App Store Review Guideline 5.1.2(i) forbids gating functionality or offering incentives to obtain the permission. It is a platform rule, not law, and a separate consent under the ePrivacy rules may still be needed.

title: Apple WebKit Intelligent Tracking Prevention and full third-party cookie blocking
takeaway: Safari 13.1 and iOS and iPadOS 13.4 completed Intelligent Tracking Prevention by blocking all cross-site cookies by default, with the Storage Access API as the only exception, and by deleting all script-writable storage (cookies, IndexedDB, LocalStorage, service worker caches) after seven days without user interaction. WebKit's tracking prevention page adds that cookies set through CNAME or IP-address cloaking are capped at seven days and JavaScript cookies on landing pages reached through link decoration at 24 hours. These are engine defaults, not law. Measurement that relies on script-written first-party storage in Safari loses returning users after seven days of Safari use without interaction, whatever consent was recorded; cookies set by the server in an HTTP response are not capped unless they arrive through CNAME or IP-address cloaking.

title: Mozilla Firefox Total Cookie Protection by default and Global Privacy Control setting
takeaway: Firefox has shipped Total Cookie Protection to all desktop users by default since 14 June 2022, confining each site's cookies to a separate jar so that third-party cookies cannot follow users across sites, on top of the list-based Enhanced Tracking Protection introduced in 2018. Global Privacy Control has been available since Firefox 120 as an opt-in setting labelled 'Tell websites not to sell or share my data'; Mozilla notes that some websites may ignore it. These are browser defaults, not law. A banner cannot assume a Firefox third-party cookie is readable, and Firefox visitors sending GPC must be handled as opt-outs wherever a law recognises the signal.

title: Brave Shields default blocking and Global Privacy Control on by default
takeaway: Brave Shields blocks third-party ads, trackers and cross-site cookies on every page by default, using EasyList, EasyPrivacy, uBlock Origin and Brave's own filter lists, and randomises the browser fingerprint. Brave has sent the Global Privacy Control signal by default since 7 October 2020, describing it as a way for users to assert legal privacy rights, with an option to turn it off in privacy settings. These are browser defaults, not law. A business that receives Sec-GPC: 1 from a Brave visitor in a state that recognises the signal must treat it as an opt-out of sale, sharing and targeted advertising.

title: W3C Tracking Preference Expression (Do Not Track), Working Group Note
takeaway: Tracking Preference Expression, published as a W3C Working Group Note on 17 January 2019, defined a DNT request header whose value 1 expressed a preference not to be tracked. The Tracking Protection Working Group closed because there had not been sufficient deployment to justify further advancement and no indication of planned support among user agents, third parties and the wider ecosystem. The header still exists in some browsers but has no defined legal effect and no cookie law requires sites to honour it. Withdrawn as a standard; Global Privacy Control (W3C Working Draft) is its successor for opt-out signalling, so do not build banner logic on DNT.

title: EDPB Website Auditing Tool
takeaway: The EDPB Website Auditing Tool, released on 29 January 2024 under the EUPL 1.2 licence through the Support Pool of Experts, lets a data protection authority, controller or processor record a visit to a website and analyse the cookies, storage and third-party requests it triggers, with full-page screenshots, import and export of analyses and searchable databases. It is free and open source and available in English, French, German, Italian and Spanish. It is a tool rather than guidance, and the EDPB states that it does not represent an official EDPB position. Run it against your own sites before and after consent to see what a regulator would see.

title: ISO/IEC 29184:2020 Online privacy notices and consent
takeaway: ISO/IEC 29184:2020, published on 2 June 2020 (edition 1, 25 pages, reviewed and confirmed in 2026), specifies controls for the content and structure of online privacy notices and for the process of obtaining, recording and withdrawing consent when personally identifiable information is collected. It is a voluntary standard: it binds no one unless adopted by contract or certification, and it does not replace the GDPR Article 7 conditions or national cookie rules. Use it as a checklist for layered notices and for the record a CMP should keep about each consent, including what the user was shown and when.

title: BfDI recognition of consent management services under section 26 TDDDG
takeaway: The BfDI runs the recognition procedure under section 26 TDDDG and sections 10 to 13 EinwV: it reviews an application, sends a draft decision to the applicant and the Land supervisory authorities with four weeks for comments, requires a security concept and independence from companies with a financial interest in consent data, and keeps a public register. The first recognition, of the service Consenter operated by Law & Innovation Technology GmbH, was granted on 17 October 2025. Recognition means the service meets the ordinance, not that any consent it stores is valid for a given site; German publishers should decide how to treat its signals alongside their own banner.

title: Microsoft Advertising consent mode requirement for UET
takeaway: Microsoft Advertising announced on 31 March 2025 that from 5 May 2025 advertisers must pass user consent signals for site visits from the EEA, the UK and Switzerland, through consent mode on the Universal Event Tracking tag or Microsoft pixels (an ad_storage parameter set to granted or denied), through the IAB TCF, or through a tag manager integration. Without a signal, advertising performance for those visitors is affected because the data is not used for optimisation. It is a platform requirement, not law; map the CMP's advertising category to ad_storage so that the tag fires only after consent.

title: European Commission acceptance of Meta's DMA commitments on personalised advertising choice
takeaway: On 8 December 2025 the European Commission announced Meta's commitment under the Digital Markets Act to give EU users of Facebook and Instagram, from January 2026, a choice between sharing all their data for fully personalised advertising and sharing limited data for an experience with more limited personalised advertising, following the Commission's April 2025 non-compliance decision on the earlier consent-or-pay model. The commitment binds Meta and changes what signals its advertising systems hold for EU users. Advertisers running the Meta Pixel and Conversions API remain responsible for their own website consent under the ePrivacy rules and the GDPR, and should verify that pixel events fire only after that consent.

title: PECR Regulation 6 (Privacy and Electronic Communications (EC Directive) Regulations 2003, SI 2003/2426), as amended by the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025
takeaway: Regulation 6(1) prohibits storing information, or gaining access to information stored, in a subscriber's or user's terminal equipment, subject to the exceptions in new Schedule A1; regulation 6(2) extends the prohibition to instigating storage or access and to collecting information automatically emitted by the device, which captures fingerprinting and pixels. It binds any person operating a website, app or connected service reaching UK users, not only controllers. Map every storage or access operation to one Schedule A1 exception (consent, transmission, strictly necessary, statistical, appearance, emergency) and document it. The substituted text applies from 5 February 2026 under SI 2026/82, regulation 2(w).

title: Data (Use and Access) Act 2025, section 112 and Schedule 12: new Schedule A1 to PECR (exceptions to the storage and access prohibition)
takeaway: Schedule 12 inserts Schedule A1 into PECR. Paragraph 2 permits storage or access where the user receives clear and comprehensive information and gives consent, which may be signified through browser or application settings; paragraphs 3 and 4 keep the transmission and strictly necessary exceptions; paragraph 5 covers collection solely for statistical purposes to improve the service; paragraph 6 covers adapting appearance or functionality to user preferences; paragraph 7 covers emergency geolocation. Paragraphs 5 and 6 require prior information, a simple free means of objecting, and no disclosure except to a party assisting with improvements. Rely on paragraph 5 only with processor-only analytics and a live objection control.

title: Data (Use and Access) Act 2025, section 115 and Schedule 13: PECR enforcement aligned with the Data Protection Act 2018
takeaway: Schedule 13 substitutes Schedule 1 to PECR and applies the Data Protection Act 2018 enforcement toolkit to regulation 6 breaches: information, assessment, interview and enforcement notices, powers of entry and penalty notices under sections 155 to 157 as modified. The maximum penalty for a regulation 6 contravention becomes the UK GDPR higher ceiling of £17.5 million or 4 per cent of worldwide annual turnover, whichever is greater, replacing the previous £500,000 cap; the former threshold of serious contravention causing substantial damage or distress falls away. It binds every person subject to PECR. Treat tag deployment as a UK GDPR-scale liability. In force from 5 February 2026 under SI 2026/82.

title: Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 (Commencement No. 6 and Transitional and Saving Provisions) Regulations 2026, SI 2026/82
takeaway: Regulation 2 brings the PECR provisions of the 2025 Act into force on 5 February 2026, including section 112 and Schedule 12 (regulation 6 and Schedule A1 exceptions), section 115 and Schedule 13 (enforcement and penalties), and section 101 on penalty notices; regulation 3 commences further provisions on 19 June 2026. It applies to every organisation subject to PECR and the UK GDPR. Use 5 February 2026 as the date from which the statistical and appearance exceptions can be relied on and from which regulation 6 breaches attract UK GDPR-level fines; the transitional provisions govern investigations opened before that date.

title: Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 (Commencement No. 9 and Transitional and Saving Provisions) Regulations 2026, SI 2026/1015: abolition of the Information Commissioner and transfer to the Information Commission
takeaway: Made on 10 September 2026, regulation 2 commences sections 118 and 119 of the 2025 Act on 30 September 2026: the office of Information Commissioner is abolished and its functions transfer to the Information Commission, a body corporate with a board of seven non-executive members and an interim chief executive. The ICO confirms it will continue to be known as the ICO operationally and that existing regulatory functions, guidance and enforcement continue. Update references in privacy notices, DPIAs and contracts to the Information Commission after that date; no change to PECR obligations follows from the renaming.

title: UK GDPR Article 4(11) and Article 7: definition and conditions for consent
takeaway: PECR consent means consent as defined in the UK GDPR: a freely given, specific, informed and unambiguous indication by statement or clear affirmative action (Article 4(11)). Article 7 requires the controller to demonstrate consent, to present the request clearly distinguishable from other matters in plain language, to allow withdrawal at any time with withdrawal as easy as giving consent, and to weigh whether access to a service is conditioned on unnecessary consent when judging whether it is freely given. It binds every controller relying on consent. Build banners so reject and withdraw match accept in effort, keep consent records, and never treat browsing or pre-ticked boxes as consent.

title: ICO Guidance on the use of storage and access technologies (final version)
takeaway: The guidance explains how PECR regulation 6 and the UK GDPR apply to cookies, tracking pixels, link decoration, local storage, device fingerprinting, scripts and tags across websites, apps and connected TV, with chapters on the five exceptions, consent in practice, online advertising, cookie walls and consent or pay, and what a simple means of objecting requires. The statistical exception covers how a service is used, not who uses it; the appearance exception excludes adapting content to inferred interests; both need information and a free objection control, and legitimate interests is unavailable for non-exempt technologies. It replaces the 2024 and 2025 drafts and applies to every organisation subject to PECR.

title: ICO consultation on the draft updated guidance on storage and access technologies (draft that replaced the 2019 cookies guidance)
takeaway: The draft, previously known as the detailed cookies guidance, widened the ICO's cookie position to all storage and access technologies, confirmed that consent must meet the UK GDPR standard, that reject must be as easy as accept, that the strictly necessary exception is judged from the user's perspective and that pixels and fingerprinting are in scope. It was open for comment until 5 pm on 21 March 2025 and was directed at every organisation deploying such technologies for UK users. Use it only to trace how the ICO's thinking developed; it was superseded by the final guidance published on 29 April 2026.

title: ICO consultation on a new chapter within the draft updated guidance on storage and access technologies (Data (Use and Access) Act exceptions)
takeaway: Opened on 7 July 2025 and closed on 26 September 2025, the consultation added a chapter explaining the statistical purposes and appearance exceptions introduced by the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025, including the information and objection conditions and the restriction on sharing statistical data beyond processors. It was addressed to website and app operators, analytics vendors and consent management platform providers serving UK users. Its content was folded into the final guidance of 29 April 2026, which supersedes it; cite the final text rather than the draft chapter.

title: ICO Guidance on the use of cookies and similar technologies (2019 detailed cookies guidance)
takeaway: Version 1.0 of 3 July 2019 set the ICO's post-GDPR cookie position: PECR consent means GDPR consent, continuing to browse is not consent, pre-ticked boxes and default-on sliders are invalid, analytics cookies are not strictly necessary and need consent, non-essential cookies must not be set before consent, third parties must be named, and cookie walls are acceptable only in limited circumstances. It applied to every operator of a website or app used from the UK and still appears in audit checklists and vendor documentation. It has been superseded by the Guidance on the use of storage and access technologies of 29 April 2026, which reflects the statistical exception for analytics.

title: ICO Consent or pay guidance
takeaway: The guidance states that consent or pay models, which offer a choice between consenting to personalised advertising, paying a fee, or leaving the service, can comply with UK data protection law where consent is freely given, assessed against four factors: power imbalance, equivalence of the core service, an appropriate fee, and privacy by design in how the choice is presented. It applies to any organisation operating or considering such a model for UK users, with additional expectations where services are likely to be accessed by children under 18 (the Children's code applies, with profiling off by default) and parental consent where consent is sought from children under 13. Document the four-factor assessment in a DPIA before launch and present both options with equal prominence.

title: ICO takes action to tackle cookie compliance across the UK's top 1,000 websites (2025 online tracking strategy)
takeaway: The announcement launched the ICO's 2025 online tracking strategy with a commitment to bring the UK's top 1,000 websites into compliance, having already assessed the top 200 and written to 134 of them about advertising cookies placed before consent and unequal accept and reject options. It targets every operator of a high-traffic UK website and the ad tech vendors behind them. Audit banners against the three ICO tests: no non-essential advertising cookies before choice, reject as easy as accept, and no cookies set after refusal.

title: ICO action secures increased cookie compliance across the UK's top 1,000 websites (campaign outcome)
takeaway: The ICO reports that 979 of the top 1,000 UK websites met its compliance checks at the most recent test, with 21 still failing; 415 passed without intervention and 564 improved after initially failing, following warning letters, investigations and 17 preliminary enforcement notices. The checks were whether advertising cookies were stored before the user could choose, whether rejecting was as easy as accepting, and whether cookies were placed despite refusal. The outcome covers sites reaching an estimated 80 per cent of UK internet users over 14. Expect periodic re-testing; keep the three checks in release testing so sites do not revert.

title: ICO reprimand: Sky Betting and Gaming (Bonne Terre Limited) for advertising cookies without consent
takeaway: The ICO found that between 10 January and 3 March 2023 Sky Betting and Gaming processed personal data through advertising cookies and shared it with ad tech companies before visitors could accept or reject them, in breach of PECR and the UK GDPR, and issued a reprimand; the company changed its banner in March 2023. The same announcement reported that 52 of 53 warned top-100 websites had made changes, leaving 99 of the top 100 offering a meaningful choice. It applies to any operator whose tags fire before consent. Verify tag sequencing on first page load and block ad tech calls until consent is recorded.

title: ICO and CMA joint position paper: Harmful design in digital markets (online choice architecture and cookie choices)
takeaway: The joint paper identifies design practices that breach data protection and consumer law, including failing to give an equal choice between accept all and reject all cookies, confusing privacy controls, persuasive language steering data sharing, bundled choices and defaults that limit control. It applies to every organisation designing online interfaces for UK consumers and records both regulators' warning that businesses which deliberately and persistently design unfairly risk enforcement. Use the paper as the UK benchmark for banner and preference-centre design and as the reference for the ICO's later reject-as-easy-as-accept enforcement tests.

title: CMA acceptance of Google's Privacy Sandbox commitments (investigation into Google's Privacy Sandbox browser changes)
takeaway: On 11 February 2022 the CMA accepted binding commitments under which Google would design and test the Privacy Sandbox with the CMA and the ICO before any final decision to remove third-party cookies from Chrome, would not self-preference its own ad tech and would limit its use of data, with a monitoring trustee appointed in March 2022. The commitments bound Google but set the timeline for every publisher and vendor planning for cookie deprecation in the UK. Google announced in July 2024 that it would retain third-party cookies with a user choice and in April 2025 that no prompt would ship. The CMA released the commitments on 17 October 2025.

title: CMA decision to release Google from the Privacy Sandbox commitments
takeaway: Following a consultation opened in June 2025 after Google abandoned third-party cookie deprecation in Chrome, the CMA decided on 17 October 2025 that it had reasonable grounds to believe its competition concerns no longer arose and released Google from all the 2022 commitments, ending the CMA and ICO oversight of Privacy Sandbox design. The decision concerns Google but removes the regulatory driver behind UK cookie deprecation planning. Plan on third-party cookies persisting in Chrome for UK users, keep consent-based tagging as the compliance baseline, and treat Privacy Sandbox APIs as optional rather than a mandated replacement.

title: ICO advice to government on potential changes to online advertising rules (PECR regulation 6 exception for low-risk advertising)
takeaway: The ICO advised the Department for Science, Innovation and Technology that regulation 6 could be amended by secondary legislation, using the power in the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025, to allow certain low-risk forms of online advertising to operate without consent where advertising is based on the context of the content viewed rather than a person's past activity, while intrusive tracking and profiling over time and across services would continue to require consent. It is advice to government, not law, and the ICO states that the existing PECR rules still apply and organisations must continue to comply. Keep consent for behavioural advertising and monitor for draft regulations.

title: Federal Act on Data Protection (FADP, SR 235.1), revised text
takeaway: The revised FADP entered into force on 1 September 2023 without a transition period. Article 6 requires that consent, where relied on, is voluntary and informed, and express for sensitive personal data and for high-risk profiling, which Article 5 defines as profiling entailing a high risk to personality or fundamental rights; Article 19 imposes a duty to inform at collection, including the countries of any disclosure abroad. Article 60 provides criminal fines of up to CHF 250,000 against the responsible individual for wilful breaches of the information duties. It binds private controllers and federal bodies; tracking needs consent only where it reaches sensitive data or high-risk profiling.

title: Telecommunications Act (TCA, SR 784.10), Article 45c: data on external equipment
takeaway: Article 45c permits the processing of data on external equipment by telecommunications transmission, which covers setting and reading cookies and similar identifiers, only where users are informed about the processing and its purpose and about the means to refuse it, or where the processing is necessary for the service. It binds every operator of a website or app reaching users in Switzerland; the FDPIC applies it cumulatively with the FADP, reads the refusal requirement as a mandatory opt-out control, and cites a fine of up to CHF 5,000 under Article 53 TCA. Provide the notice and a refusal control before any non-necessary cookie is set.

title: FDPIC Guidelines on data processing using cookies and similar technologies, version 1.1
takeaway: Version 1.1 of 6 October 2025 replaces version 1.0 of 22 January 2025 and sets out how the FDPIC supervises cookies, pixels and similar technologies under the FADP, the Data Protection Ordinance and Article 45c TCA: necessary cookies need information only; other non-essential cookies justified by overriding interests need information and a mandatory opt-out; express consent is required for sensitive data, high-risk profiling, any profiling by federal bodies and unexpected uses that seriously intrude, including paid access for multiple embedded advertising third parties and location profiling. Banners must not use pre-ticked boxes or dark patterns; cookie paywalls need a proportionate price. Penalties reach CHF 250,000 (FADP) and CHF 5,000 (TCA).

title: FDPIC Factsheet on the use of cookies and similar technologies (for internet users)
takeaway: The factsheet, published on 31 March 2026, is the FDPIC's awareness document for internet users and complements rather than replaces the operator-facing Guidelines of 6 October 2025. It explains what cookies do, encourages data-minimalist use, warns against blanket acceptance of all cookies and points users to opt-in and opt-out controls and their rights of control and choice. It creates no obligations for operators but signals the FDPIC's expectation that refusal and withdrawal controls are easy to find and use. Use it to anticipate the complaints the FDPIC will receive and to test that the refusal path on Swiss-facing sites works as the factsheet describes.

title: Norway: Electronic Communications Act (ekomloven) section 3-15 on cookies and similar technologies, with Nkom and Datatilsynet joint supervision
takeaway: The new ekomloven, in force from 1 January 2025, provides in section 3-15 that use of cookies and similar technologies requires consent valid under the GDPR: voluntary, specific, informed, unambiguous, given by active action, documented and easily withdrawable, replacing the former section 2-7b under which browser default settings counted as consent. Supervision is shared by Nkom and Datatilsynet from the same date. It binds every operator of a website or app directed at users in Norway, whether or not established there. Retire any reliance on browser settings for Norwegian traffic and apply the same opt-in banner standard as under the EU rules, with the Norwegian regulators as enforcement contacts.

title: Norway Datatilsynet guidance page on cookies and information capsules (informasjonskapsler)
takeaway: Datatilsynet's cookie page states that consent to cookies must be GDPR-valid consent, so that browser settings alone do not suffice, and explains the interaction between the cookie rule in ekomloven and the personal data rules in personopplysningsloven and the GDPR, both of which apply at once. It is addressed to Norwegian website and app operators and to foreign operators serving Norwegian users. Read it together with Nkom's page on section 3-15, since the Datatilsynet page still cites the former section 2-7b and Nkom as sole supervisor; the operative rule since 1 January 2025 is section 3-15 with joint supervision.

title: Turkey: KVKK Guideline on Cookie Practices (Çerez Uygulamaları Hakkında Rehber)
takeaway: The Personal Data Protection Board's guideline applies Law No. 6698 to cookies: strictly necessary cookies may be used without explicit consent, while cookies for advertising, profiling and non-essential analytics require explicit consent under Article 5 of the Law, with information duties under Article 10 met through a cookie policy and banner, and cross-border transfers through cookies subject to the Law's transfer rules. It applies to every data controller whose website or app processes data of users in Turkey. Provide a Turkish-language banner with granular explicit opt-in for non-essential cookies, no pre-ticked boxes, and a cookie policy listing each cookie, purpose and duration.

title: Turkey: Personal Data Protection Board decision on Amazon Turkey (cookies and marketing without explicit consent), decision no. 2020/173
takeaway: The Board found that Amazon Turkey processed personal data through cookies and sent marketing communications without obtaining explicit consent and without adequate information, in breach of Articles 5, 10 and 12 of Law No. 6698, and imposed administrative fines totalling TRY 1,200,000: TRY 1,100,000 under Article 12 for failing to take the technical and organisational measures that would have prevented processing without explicit consent, and TRY 100,000 under Article 10 for failing to inform users about the cookies. The decision binds the addressee and sets the Board's position for all controllers using cookies on Turkish users. It remains the reference enforcement precedent that the 2022 Guideline on Cookie Practices later codified; treat cookie consent in Turkey as an opt-in explicit consent regime.

title: California Consumer Privacy Act as amended by the CPRA, Cal. Civ. Code 1798.100 et seq. (sections 1798.120, 1798.135, 1798.155)
takeaway: Section 1798.120 gives consumers the right to direct a business not to sell or share their personal information. Section 1798.135(a) requires a clear and conspicuous homepage link titled Do Not Sell or Share My Personal Information plus a Limit the Use of My Sensitive Personal Information link, or one consolidated link; 1798.135(b) lets a business omit the links if it honours an opt-out preference signal. Section 1798.120(c) requires opt-in under 16; section 1798.155 sets fines of up to $2,500 per violation and $7,500 for intentional violations or those involving the data of consumers known to be under 16, amounts the California Privacy Protection Agency adjusts for inflation ($2,663 and $7,988 from 1 January 2025). Route ad tech sharing, the link and the signal to one suppression path. Current text as amended by AB 3286.

title: CCPA Regulations, Cal. Code Regs. Title 11, Division 6, Chapter 1 (final text of 29 March 2023)
takeaway: The 2023 text established the operative rules behind the statute: section 7004 bans dark patterns and requires symmetry in choice, so declining must take no more steps than accepting; sections 7013 to 7015 govern the Do Not Sell or Share link, the Limit the Use link and the Alternative Opt-out Link; section 7025 makes opt-out preference signals mandatory to process; section 7026 governs opt-out requests. It binds every business subject to the CCPA and its service providers and contractors. Use it to understand the reasoning behind current enforcement. Superseded as a document by the consolidated regulations text approved on 22 September 2025 and effective 1 January 2026.

title: CCPA Updates, Cybersecurity Audits, Risk Assessments, ADMT and Insurance Regulations (approved text, effective 1 January 2026)
takeaway: Approved by the Office of Administrative Law on 22 September 2025, the amended regulations took effect on 1 January 2026. Section 7025(c)(6) now requires a business to display whether it has processed a consumer's opt-out preference signal, replacing the earlier permissive wording. Risk assessments are required for processing that presents significant risk, including selling or sharing personal information, with documentation due to the agency by 1 April 2028; ADMT obligations apply from 1 January 2027; cybersecurity audits are staggered from 1 April 2028 by revenue. It binds all CCPA businesses. Add the signal-status indicator to the banner and log selling and sharing through cookies in the risk assessment.

title: Cal. Code Regs. Title 11, section 7025, Opt-Out Preference Signals
takeaway: Section 7025(b) requires a business that sells or shares personal information to process any opt-out preference signal sent in a commonly used format such as an HTTP header, and 7025(c) requires it to treat the signal as a valid opt-out for that browser or device and any associated consumer profile, without demanding extra information. Section 7025(e) and (f) let a business drop the Do Not Sell or Share link only if it processes the signal frictionlessly: no fee, no changed experience, no pop-up. It binds every CCPA business. Read Global Privacy Control before any tags fire. Amended from 1 January 2026 to require display of the signal's processing status.

title: AB 566, California Opt Me Out Act (Chapter 465, Statutes of 2025), Cal. Civ. Code 1798.136
takeaway: Chaptered on 8 October 2025, the act adds section 1798.136 to the Civil Code and requires a business that develops or maintains a browser to include a setting, easy for a reasonable person to locate and configure, that lets the consumer send an opt-out preference signal. The California Privacy Protection Agency may adopt implementing regulations, and browser developers are not liable for violations by businesses receiving the signal. The obligation is operative from 1 January 2027 and binds browser vendors, not website operators. Expect signal volumes to rise sharply after that date and size opt-out handling accordingly.

title: Delete Act (SB 362), Cal. Civ. Code 1798.99.86, accessible deletion mechanism
takeaway: Section 1798.99.86 required the California Privacy Protection Agency to establish, by 1 January 2026, a free mechanism through which a consumer submits a single verifiable request that every registered data broker delete their personal information. From 1 August 2026 each data broker must access the mechanism at least every 45 days, delete within 45 days of receipt, direct service providers and contractors to do the same, and undergo an independent compliance audit every three years from 1 January 2028.
